writtenQuestions.text: Can a non-physical quantity be measured? If yes, then how?
modelAnswer: A non-physical quantity cannot be measured using tools and instruments.
It can be described qualitatively or compared using pre-determined criteria, indices or survey techniques.

example.answer: Length—ruler; time duration—clock; temperature—thermometer. All are physical quantities.

explain.title: Physical quantities
explain.body: “Some of these can be measured directly and indirectly using some tools and instruments such as length of an object using a ruler, time duration of an event using a clock, the temperature (the degree of hotness) of somebody using a thermometer. They are called physical quantities.” A physical quantity can be measured, and physics uses physical quantities to express its laws and principles.

explain.title: Non-physical quantities
explain.body: “Other quantities quoted above such as love, affection, fear, wisdom, and beauty cannot be measured using tools and instruments.” These are non-physical quantities. They may be described qualitatively or compared using criteria, indices or surveys.

explain.title: Compare the two types
explain.body: Physical quantities can be measured and have a numerical value and a unit. Non-physical quantities cannot be measured with instruments. For example, length is physical, while fear is non-physical.

mistakes: Do not call something physical just because it can be described in words; it must be measurable with tools or instruments.
Do not confuse a survey or agreed criterion with direct measurement by a physical instrument.
When giving examples, use measurable quantities such as length, volume, density, time or temperature for physical quantities.
Do not claim that a non-physical quantity has a measurement unit or instrument.

modelAnswer: A standard unit ensures that measurements made by different people give the same result.
It avoids confusion caused by measurements using different-sized hands, arms or steps.

explain.title: Base quantities
explain.body: Scientists have selected arbitrarily some quantities to play a key role. They are called base quantities.

explain.title: Derived quantities
explain.body: All the quantities which can be described in terms of one or more base quantities are called derived physical quantities. For example, speed depends on distance and time, and density is described in terms of mass and volume.

explain.title: Measurement and units
explain.body: A measurement is a process of comparison of an unknown quantity with a widely accepted standard quantity. The standard of measurement is called a unit.

explain.title: Two parts of a measurement
explain.body: A measurement consists of two parts, a number and a unit. A measurement without unit is meaningless.

mistakes: Calling speed a base quantity instead of a derived quantity; speed depends on distance and time.
Giving examples without labelling which are base and which are derived.
Writing only a number for a measurement and leaving out its unit.
Saying a standard unit is needed only for convenience; explain that it helps different people obtain the same result and prevents confusion.

explain.title: SI helps everyone measure in a common way
explain.body: SI is the international system of units. Using it helps scientists share and compare observations and results easily.

explain.title: The seven base units
explain.body: The seven base units are metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K), ampere (A), candela (cd) and mole (mol). Their values are fixed with reference to international standards.

explain.title: Derived units come from base units
explain.body: The units which can be expressed in terms of base units are called derived units. For example, area is measured in square metres (m²), and speed in metres per second (m s⁻¹).

explain.title: Prefixes show powers of ten
explain.body: Prefixes are the words or symbols added before SI units, such as milli, centi and kilo. They make very large or small quantities more convenient to write.

explain.title: Convert carefully
explain.body: Use the prefix value to convert a measurement. For example, 3000 g = 3000/1000 kg = 3 kg. Keep the unit in your answer.

mistakes: Mixing up unit symbols, such as writing K for kilo instead of kelvin; symbols are case-sensitive.
Forgetting that prefixes represent powers of ten, or using the wrong exponent when converting.
Changing the number but leaving out the unit in the final answer.
Confusing base units with derived units: kilogram is a base unit, while newton and pascal are derived units.
Writing a prefix symbol with the wrong case, such as M for milli instead of m.

explain.title: What scientific notation means
explain.body: It is short way of representing very large or very small numbers. The numerical part of the quantity is written as a number from 1 to 9 multiplied by whole number powers of 10.

explain.title: Writing a large number
explain.body: To write numbers using scientific notation, move the decimal point until only one non-zero digit remains on the left. Count the places moved: moving the decimal to the left gives a positive exponent of 10. For example, 138,000,000 km = 1.38 × 10⁸ km.

explain.title: Writing a small number
explain.body: For a small number, move the decimal point to the right until one non-zero digit remains on the left. The number of places moved to the right is expressed as a negative exponent of 10. For example, 0.000,000,000,052 m = 5.2 × 10⁻¹¹ m.

explain.title: Calculating with powers of 10
explain.body: For addition or subtraction, first write the terms with the same power of 10. For multiplication, multiply the coefficients and add the exponents. For division, divide the coefficients and subtract the denominator exponent from the numerator exponent.

mistakes: Using a positive exponent when the decimal point moved to the right, or a negative exponent when it moved to the left.
Adding or subtracting coefficients before making the powers of 10 equal.
Forgetting to add exponents in multiplication or subtract exponents in division.
Leaving a coefficient such as 24 or 0.35 in the final answer instead of normalizing it to a value from 1 to 9.
Dropping the unit or giving an incorrect unit after multiplying or dividing quantities.

explain.title: Least count
explain.body: Least count is the smallest measurement that can be taken accurately with an instrument. The metre rule's least count is 1 mm. In this section, Vernier Callipers has a least count of 0.1 mm and a micrometer screw gauge has a least count of 0.01 mm.

explain.title: Read the ruler from above
explain.body: Parallax error is due to incorrect position of eye when taking measurements. It can be avoided by keeping eye perpendicular to the scale reading. In Fig. 1.1, point B gives the correct reading.

explain.title: Vernier Callipers
explain.body: It is an instrument used to measure small lengths down to 1/10th of a millimetre. It can be used to measure the thickness, diameter, width or depth of an object. The two scales on it are: (a) A main scale which has marking of 1mm each. (b) A Vernier (sliding) scale of length 9 mm and it is divided into 10 equal parts.

explain.title: Zero error
explain.body: If the zeros of the main scale and Vernier scale do not exactly coincide when the jaws are joined, the instrument has zero error. A Vernier zero to the right of the main-scale zero reads slightly more, so subtract the zero error. A Vernier zero to the left reads slightly less, so add the zero error.

explain.title: Micrometer screw gauge
explain.body: A screw gauge measures very small lengths such as the diameter of a wire or the thickness of a metal sheet. Its least count is the pitch divided by the number of divisions on the circular scale.

mistakes: Reading a ruler from an angle instead of keeping the eye directly above the scale causes parallax error.
Forgetting to multiply the smaller-scale reading by the least count loses marks.
Adding the Vernier or circular-scale contribution incorrectly, instead of adding it to the main-scale reading, gives the wrong measurement.
Using the wrong correction direction for zero error: subtract for a Vernier zero to the right and add for a Vernier zero to the left.
Leaving out units or writing a reading with more precision than the instrument supports.

explain.title: Measuring cylinder
explain.body: “It is a cylinder made of glass or transparent plastic with a scale divided in cubic centimetres (cm³ or cc) or millilitres (mL) marked on it. It is used to find the volume of liquids and non-dissolvable solids.” Place it on a horizontal surface and read the liquid level at eye height.

explain.title: Meniscus and reading water
explain.body: “The meniscus is the top level of the liquid surface.” Water curves downward and its surface is called concave. For water, take the reading at the bottom edge of the surface. Mercury curves upward, making a convex surface, so take its reading at the top edge.

explain.title: Volume by displacement
explain.body: Note the liquid reading before and after placing a non-dissolvable solid in it. The difference between the readings is the solid’s volume. If the body does not fit in the measuring cylinder, use a displacement can: collect the overflowing liquid and measure it in a measuring cylinder. That volume equals the solid’s volume.

explain.title: Avoid a wrong reading
explain.body: Keep the cylinder level on a horizontal surface. Keep your eye in front and in line with the lower meniscus of water; looking from above or below gives an incorrect reading.

mistakes: Reading the top edge of water’s meniscus instead of its bottom edge.
Looking at the meniscus from above or below instead of keeping the eye level with it.
Taking a reading while the cylinder is tilted or held off a horizontal surface.
Giving the final liquid reading as the solid’s volume instead of subtracting the initial reading.
Forgetting that the overflow’s volume, not its mass, equals the solid’s volume in the displacement can method.

writtenQuestions.text: Identify and explain the reasons for human errors, random errors and systematic errors in experiments.
modelAnswer: Human errors occur due to personal performance, such as difficulty estimating a pointer's position or reaction time when starting or stopping a clock.
Random errors occur when repeated measurements give different values under the same conditions because of unknown, unpredictable causes, such as changes in temperature or air pressure.
Systematic errors arise from a definite cause and produce a consistent difference in readings; examples include zero error, poor calibration or incorrect marking.

explain.title: Measurements have errors
explain.body: Measurements using tools and instruments are never perfect. They can differ from their true values, so a scientific measurement should indicate the estimated error.

explain.title: Human errors
explain.body: “They occur due to personal performance.” Examples include difficulty reading a pointer, using a faulty procedure to read a scale, or reaction time when starting or stopping a clock. Training, proper technique and digital instruments can help reduce them.

explain.title: Systematic errors
explain.body: “They refer to an effect that influences all measurements of particular measurements equally.” A definite cause, such as zero error or poor calibration, produces a consistent difference in readings. Comparing with a more accurate instrument can help, and a correction factor can be applied.

explain.title: Random errors
explain.body: “It is said to occur when repeated measurements of a quantity give different values under the same conditions.” Unknown, unpredictable causes, including environmental changes, can produce them. Take several readings and use their average or mean to reduce their effect.

explain.title: Recognise the cause
explain.body: A personal reading or handling problem points to human error; a definite, consistent instrument effect points to systematic error; unpredictable variation between readings points to random error.

mistakes: Calling every incorrect reading a human error: first identify the cause of the error.
Mixing up systematic and random errors: systematic errors affect readings consistently, while random errors vary unpredictably.
Giving only the name of an error when asked to explain it; include the cause or a suitable example.
Saying that averaging removes every type of error; the textbook recommends several readings and their mean to reduce random errors.

steps.why: The smallest division is 0.1 cm, so its midpoint divides it into two equal parts.

steps.text: If the end does not touch or cross the midpoint, record the previous division; if it touches or has crossed the midpoint, record the next division.

example.question: A straight line is measured with a metre rule calibrated in millimetres. Its end lies between 10.3 cm and 10.4 cm. How is the reading chosen, and what is the maximum uncertainty?

explain.title: Measurements are not perfect
explain.body: There is no such thing as a perfect measurement. Whenever a physical quantity is measured except counting, there is inevitably some uncertainty about its determined value due to some instrument. The instrument's smallest division limits how accurately you can read it.

explain.title: Uncertainty on an analogue scale
explain.body: For the metre-rule example, the smallest division is 0.1 cm. The maximum uncertainty is half of this, or ±0.05 cm. Use the midpoint convention: record the previous division if the endpoint is before the midpoint, and the next division if it touches or crosses the midpoint.

explain.title: Digital readings and repeated readings
explain.body: With digital scale, this is reflected in fluctuation of the last digit. For small lengths or short time intervals, take multiple readings and find their average to reduce uncertainty.

explain.title: Significant figures
explain.body: The uncertainty or accuracy in the value of a measured quantity can be indicated conveniently by using significant figures.

mistakes: Using the whole smallest division instead of half of it when stating the maximum uncertainty.
Ignoring the midpoint convention when deciding whether to record the previous or next division.
Treating every digit on a digital display as equally certain instead of noticing fluctuation in the last digit.
Using just one reading when several readings and their average could reduce uncertainty.
Counting leading zeros as significant digits.

writtenQuestions.text: Differentiate between precision and accuracy of a measurement with examples.
modelAnswer: Precision of a measurement refers to how close together a group of measurements actually are to each other.
Accuracy of a measurement refers to how close the measured value is to some accepted or true value.
Arrows clustered together away from the bullseye are precise but not accurate.
Arrows clustered at the bullseye are both accurate and precise.
Therefore, precision compares measurements with each other, while accuracy compares a measurement with the true value.

explain.title: Precision
explain.body: Precision describes how close a group of measurements is to one another. If repeated readings are tightly grouped, they are precise.

explain.title: Accuracy
explain.body: Accuracy describes how close a measured value is to an accepted or true value. A set of readings can be precise but still miss the true value.

explain.title: The instrument and its least count
explain.body: The instrument used determines precision. The smaller the least count, the more precise the measurement. Smaller physical quantities need more precise instruments.

explain.title: Significant figures and accuracy

explain.title: Timing devices
explain.body: The textbook lists different timing devices for different intervals. For example, a digital stopwatch measures short intervals to ±0.01 s, while an analogue stopwatch measures them to ±0.1 s.

mistakes: Do not say precision means closeness to the true value; that is accuracy.
Do not assume that readings close to one another must also be accurate.
Do not forget that a smaller least count means a more precise measurement.
Do not count leading zeros as significant figures, or leave out a trailing decimal zero that is significant.
When explaining the target example, compare arrows with each other for precision and with the bullseye for accuracy.

explain.body: Significant figures are the accurately known digits and first doubtful digit in any measurement. When rounding, keep the number of significant figures asked for, then inspect the next digit.

explain.title: Digits below or above 5
explain.body: Your textbook says: “If the last digit is more than 5, the retained digit is increased by one and if it is less than 5, it is retained as such.” So a next digit of 1, 2, 3 or 4 leaves the last kept digit unchanged; a next digit of 6, 7, 8 or 9 increases it by one.

explain.title: When the next digit is exactly 5
explain.body: Your textbook gives this rule: “If the number before the 5 is odd, one is added to the last digit retained. If the number before the 5 is even, it remains the same.” For example, 4.45 rounds to 4.4 at two significant figures, while 4.55 rounds to 4.6.

explain.title: Physical quantities and units
explain.body: A physical quantity can be measured and expressed using a number and a unit. Base quantities are independent; derived quantities are formed from base quantities. The SI base units are metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), ampere (A), kelvin (K), mole (mol) and candela (cd).

explain.title: Choosing instruments and reading them
explain.body: Choose an instrument suited to the size being measured. Vernier Callipers use a main scale and Vernier scale; a micrometer screw gauge is useful for very small thicknesses. Read scales with the eye level with the mark or meniscus to avoid parallax error.

explain.title: Prefixes and scientific notation
explain.body: Prefixes such as kilo, milli, micro and nano make very large or small quantities easier to write. Scientific notation writes a number as a coefficient from 1 to 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

explain.title: Significant digits and calculations
explain.body: Significant digits communicate the precision of a measurement. Leading zeros are not significant; zeros between non-zero digits and trailing decimal zeros are significant. In addition and subtraction, align powers of ten; in multiplication and division, combine powers.

explain.title: Errors, precision and accuracy
explain.body: Human errors come from the observer. Random errors vary unpredictably, while systematic errors create a consistent shift. Precision is agreement between repeated measurements; accuracy is closeness to the true value.

mistakes: Choosing an instrument that is too coarse for the size being measured.
Looking at a scale or meniscus from above or below, causing parallax error.
Writing a measurement without its unit or using a unit for the wrong quantity.
Adding or subtracting numbers in scientific notation before making their powers of ten the same.
Counting leading zeros as significant digits or ignoring a trailing decimal zero.
Forgetting to convert units before substituting into a formula, especially kilometres to metres or centimetres cubed to metres cubed.
Reporting an answer with unjustified precision or omitting the requested SI prefix.

solutions.question: Can a non-physical quantity be measured? If yes, then how?

Its physical effects may be measured, but this does not measure the non-physical quantity itself.

solutions.question: What is measurement? Name its two parts.
steps: Measurement is the process of comparing an unknown quantity with a standard quantity of the same kind.
The two parts of a measurement are a numerical value and a unit.
solutions.answer: Measurement is comparison with a standard quantity; its two parts are a numerical value and a unit.

solutions.question: Why do we need a standard unit for measurements?
steps: A standard unit gives the same value for a measurement everywhere and at all times.
It makes measurements uniform and allows them to be understood and compared by everyone.
solutions.answer: Standard units are needed to make measurements uniform and universally understood and comparable.

solutions.question: Write the name of 3 base quantities and 3 derived quantities.

solutions.question: Why prefix is used? Name three sub-multiple and three multiple prefixes with their symbols.

Three multiple prefixes are kilo (k), 10³; mega (M), 10⁶; and giga (G), 10⁹.
solutions.answer: Prefixes express large or small measurements conveniently; examples are milli (m), micro (μ), nano (n), kilo (k), mega (M) and giga (G).

solutions.question: What is meant by: 5 pm
steps: The prefix p (pico) means 10⁻¹², and m is the symbol for metre.
Therefore, 5 pm means 5 picometres, or 5 × 10⁻¹² m.
solutions.answer: 5 pm means 5 picometres (5 × 10⁻¹² m).

solutions.question: What is meant by: 15 ns

Therefore, 15 ns means 15 × 10⁻⁹ seconds.

Therefore, 5 fs means 5 × 10⁻¹⁵ seconds.
solutions.answer: 5 femtoseconds = 5 × 10⁻¹⁵ s.

solutions.question: For what purpose, a Vernier Callipers is used?
steps: A Vernier Callipers is used to measure small lengths accurately.
It is used to measure the external and internal diameters of objects and the depth of a vessel.
solutions.answer: A Vernier Callipers measures small lengths, diameters and depths accurately.

solutions.question: Name its two main parts.

solutions.question: How is least count found?
steps: The least count is found by dividing the value of one main scale division by the total number of divisions on the Vernier scale.
Least count = value of one main scale division ÷ number of Vernier scale divisions.
solutions.answer: Least count = value of one main scale division ÷ number of Vernier scale divisions.

solutions.question: What is meant by zero error?
steps: When the jaws of a Vernier Callipers are closed, the reading should be zero.
If the zero of the Vernier scale does not coincide with the zero of the main scale, the instrument has zero error.
solutions.answer: Zero error is the non-zero reading shown by a Vernier Callipers when its jaws are closed.

Vernier scale reading = coinciding Vernier division × least count.

solutions.question: The minimum main scale reading of a micrometer screw gauge is 1 mm and there are 100 divisions on the circular scale. When thimble is rotated once, 1 mm is its measurement on the main scale. What is the least count of the instrument? The reading for thickness of a steel rod as shown in the figure.  What is the thickness of the rod?
steps: Given: Pitch of screw = 1 mm; number of divisions on circular scale = 100; main scale reading = 0 mm; circular scale reading = 70 divisions.
Required: Least count and thickness of the steel rod.
Least count = Pitch of screw ÷ Number of divisions on circular scale.
Least count = 1 mm ÷ 100 = 0.01 mm.
Thickness = Main scale reading + (Circular scale reading × Least count).
Thickness = 0 mm + (70 × 0.01 mm) = 0.70 mm.
solutions.answer: Least count = 0.01 mm; thickness of the rod = 0.70 mm

solutions.question: You are provided a metre scale and a bundle of pencils; how can the diameter of a pencil be measured using the metre scale with the same precision as that of Vernier Callipers? Describe briefly.
steps: Place 10 pencils parallel to one another and tightly together in a row.
Measure the total width of the 10 pencils with the metre scale.
Divide the measured width by 10 to find the diameter of one pencil.
Since the metre scale can measure to 1 mm, measuring 10 pencils gives a precision of 1 mm ÷ 10 = 0.1 mm, the same as that of Vernier Callipers.
solutions.answer: Measure 10 pencils together and divide their total width by 10; the diameter is obtained with a precision of 0.1 mm.

solutions.question: The end of a metre scale is worn out. Where will you place a pencil to find the length?
steps: Place one end of the pencil at a clear mark on the metre scale, such as the 1 cm mark, instead of at the worn-out end.
Read the mark at the other end of the pencil.
Subtract the starting reading from the final reading to find the length.
solutions.answer: Start the pencil at a clear scale mark, such as 1 cm, and subtract that reading from the final reading.

solutions.question: Why is it better to place the object close to the metre scale?
steps: Placing the object close to the metre scale reduces parallax error when taking the reading.
solutions.answer: It reduces parallax error.

solutions.question: Why a standard unit is needed to measure a quantity correctly?
steps: A standard unit has the same value for everyone and everywhere.
It allows measurements to be compared correctly and avoids confusion caused by different units.
solutions.answer: A standard unit is needed so measurements are uniform and can be compared correctly.

solutions.question: Suggest some natural phenomena that could serve as a reasonably accurate time standard.
steps: The rotation of the Earth about its axis is a natural periodic phenomenon that can be used as a time standard.
The revolution of the Earth around the Sun can also be used as a time standard.
The revolution of the Moon around the Earth is another natural periodic phenomenon that can serve as a time standard.
solutions.answer: The Earth’s rotation, the Earth’s revolution around the Sun, and the Moon’s revolution around the Earth can serve as natural time standards.

solutions.question: It is difficult to locate the meniscus in a wider vessel. Why?
steps: In a wider vessel, the meniscus has very little curvature and appears almost flat.
Therefore, it is difficult to locate its lowest point accurately.
solutions.answer: The meniscus is difficult to locate in a wider vessel because it appears almost flat.

solutions.question: Which instrument can be used to measure: (i) internal diameter of a test tube

Its inside jaws are placed against the inner walls of the test tube.
solutions.answer: Vernier callipers.

solutions.answer: The depth gauge of Vernier callipers.

solutions.question: What is meant by base and derived quantities? Give the names and symbols of SI base units.
steps: A base quantity is an independent physical quantity that cannot be expressed in terms of other physical quantities.
A derived quantity is one that is expressed in terms of base quantities.

The SI base quantities and their units are: length—metre (m); mass—kilogram (kg); time—second (s); electric current—ampere (A); temperature—kelvin (K); amount of substance—mole (mol); and luminous intensity—candela (cd).
solutions.answer: Base quantities are independent; derived quantities are expressed in terms of them. The SI base units are m, kg, s, A, K, mol and cd.

solutions.question: Give three examples of derived unit in SI. How are they derived from base units? Describe briefly.
steps: Area is a derived quantity; its SI unit is square metre (m²), obtained from length × length.
Volume is a derived quantity; its SI unit is cubic metre (m³), obtained from length × length × length.
Speed is a derived quantity; its SI unit is metre per second (m s⁻¹), obtained from distance ÷ time.
solutions.answer: Examples are area (m²), volume (m³) and speed (m s⁻¹), derived from SI base units.

solutions.question: State the similarities and differences between Vernier Callipers and micrometer screw gauge.
steps: Similarities: Both instruments are used to measure small lengths accurately.
Both have a main scale and an auxiliary scale, and a measurement is obtained by combining readings from the two scales.
Differences: Vernier callipers use a sliding Vernier scale and can measure external and internal diameters and depths.
A micrometer screw gauge uses the rotation of a screw to measure small thicknesses or diameters, such as the diameter of a wire.
A micrometer screw gauge generally has a smaller least count and is more precise than Vernier callipers.
solutions.answer: Both measure small lengths using main and auxiliary scales; Vernier callipers measure internal or external dimensions and depths, while a micrometer screw gauge measures small thicknesses or diameters more precisely.

solutions.question: Identify and explain the reasons for human errors, random errors and systematic errors in experiments.
steps: Human errors are caused by carelessness or by using an instrument incorrectly, such as reading a scale from the wrong position.
Random errors arise from unpredictable changes in experimental conditions or observations; they may make readings greater or smaller than the true value.
Systematic errors arise from a fault in an instrument or an incorrect experimental method, such as a zero error.
A systematic error affects readings in the same direction each time, making them consistently higher or lower than the true value.
solutions.answer: Human errors result from mistakes, random errors from unpredictable variations, and systematic errors from instrument faults or an incorrect method.

solutions.question: Differentiate between precision and accuracy of a measurement with examples.
steps: Accuracy is the closeness of a measured value to the true or actual value.
Precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to one another, or the degree of refinement of a measurement.

For example, if the actual length is 10.0 cm, a measurement of 10.0 cm is accurate; repeated measurements of 9.5 cm, 9.5 cm and 9.6 cm are precise because they are close to one another, but they are not accurate.
solutions.answer: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated measurements to one another.

solutions.question: Calculate the number of seconds in a day and state your answer using SI prefixes.
steps: Given: 1 day = 24 h; 1 h = 3600 s.
Required: Number of seconds in 1 day.
Formula: time = number of hours × 3600 s.
Substitution: time = 24 × 3600 s.
Working: time = 86,400 s = 86.4 × 10³ s.
Since 1 ks = 10³ s, time = 86.4 ks.

solutions.question: Calculate the number of seconds in a week and state your answer using SI prefixes.
steps: Given: 1 week = 7 days; 1 day = 24 h; 1 h = 3600 s.
Required: Number of seconds in 1 week.
Formula: time = number of days × 24 × 3600 s.
Substitution: time = 7 × 24 × 3600 s.
Working: time = 604,800 s = 604.8 × 10³ s.
Since 1 ks = 10³ s, time = 604.8 ks.

solutions.question: Calculate the number of seconds in a month and state your answer using SI prefixes.
steps: Given: 1 month = 30 days; 1 day = 24 h; 1 h = 3600 s.
Required: Number of seconds in 1 month.
Formula: time = number of days × 24 × 3600 s.
Substitution: time = 30 × 24 × 3600 s.
Working: time = 2,592,000 s = 2.592 × 10⁶ s.
Since 1 Ms = 10⁶ s, time = 2.592 Ms.

solutions.question: State the answers of problem 1.1 in scientific notation.
steps: Seconds in a day: 86,400 s = 8.64 × 10⁴ s.
Seconds in a week: 604,800 s = 6.048 × 10⁵ s.
Seconds in a month (30 days): 2,592,000 s = 2.592 × 10⁶ s.

solutions.question: Solve the following addition or subtraction. State your answers in scientific notation. 4 × 10⁻⁴ kg + 3 × 10⁻⁵ kg
steps: Given: 4 × 10⁻⁴ kg + 3 × 10⁻⁵ kg.
Required: Sum in scientific notation.

definitions.text: Some of these can be measured directly and indirectly using some tools and instruments such as length of an object using a ruler, time duration of an event using a clock, the temperature (the degree of hotness) of somebody using a thermometer. They are called physical quantities.
Other quantities quoted above such as love, affection, fear, wisdom, and beauty cannot be measured using tools and instruments. They often pertain to the perception or interpretation of the observer.
Out of these, the scientists have selected arbitrarily some quantities to play a key role. They are called base quantities.
All the quantities which can be described in terms of one or more base quantities are called derived physical quantities.
A measurement is a process of comparison of an unknown quantity with a widely accepted standard quantity.
This standard of measurement is known as a unit.
The units which can be expressed in terms of base units are called derived units.
Prefixes are the words or symbols added before SI unit such as milli, centi, kilo, mega, giga (Table 1.4).
It is short way of representing very large or very small numbers.
Least count is the smallest measurement that can be taken accurately with an instrument.
If the metre ruler is read from an angle, such as from point A or C, the object will appear to be of different length. This is known as parallax error.
If on joining the jaws A and B, the zeros of the main scale and Vernier scale do not exactly coincide with each other then there is an error in the instrument called zero error.
In any measurement, the accurately known digits and the first doubtful digit are known-as significant figures.

definitions.term: Significant-figure rule for zeros between digits
definitions.text: A zero between two digits is considered significant. For example in 5.06m, the number of significant figures is 3.
Zeros on the left side of the measured value are not significant. For example, in 0.0034 m, the number of significant figures is 2.

definitions.term: Significant-figure rule for zeros after a decimal
definitions.text: Zeros on the right side of a decimal are considered significant. For example, in 2.40 mm the significant digits are 3.
If numbers are recorded in scientific notation, then all the digits before the exponent are significant. For example, in 3.50 × 10⁴m, the significant figures are 3.

To write numbers using scientific notation, move the decimal point until only one non-zero digit remains on the left. Then count the number of places through which the decimal point is moved and use this number as the power or exponents of 10.

When rounding off numbers to a certain number of significant figures, do so to the nearest value. If the last digit is more than 5, the retained digit is increased by one and if it is less than 5, it is retained as such.

formulas.use: State a measured quantity; number is dimensionless and the unit is the relevant unit of that quantity.
Find area from two lengths (length and breadth in m; area in m²).
Find speed from distance and time (speed in m s⁻¹, distance in m, time in s).
Convert one day to seconds (day is a time interval; s is the SI unit of time; k = 10³).
Convert one week to seconds (week and day are time intervals; s is the SI unit of time; k = 10³).
Use the exercise’s 30-day month to convert a month to seconds (month and day are time intervals; s is the SI unit of time; M = 10⁶).
Write a number in scientific notation; x has the unit of the measured quantity, while a and n are dimensionless.

formulas.formula: For addition or subtraction: a × 10ⁿ ± b × 10ⁿ = (a ± b) × 10ⁿ
formulas.use: Add or subtract values after making their powers of 10 equal; the quantities must have the same unit.
Multiply values in scientific notation; the resulting unit is the product of the units of the two quantities.
Divide values in scientific notation; the resulting unit is the numerator unit divided by the denominator unit.

formulas.formula: Least count of Vernier Callipers = 1 main-scale division − 1 Vernier-scale division
formulas.use: Find Vernier Callipers least count (both scale divisions must use the same length unit; least count is in that unit).

formulas.formula: Length = main-scale reading + (least count × Vernier-scale reading)
formulas.use: Find an observed Vernier Callipers length (readings and least count in the same length unit; Vernier-scale reading is a number of divisions).

formulas.formula: Least count of screw gauge = pitch ÷ number of circular-scale divisions
formulas.use: Find micrometer screw gauge least count (pitch and least count in mm or m; number of divisions is dimensionless).

formulas.formula: Thickness = main-scale reading + (circular-scale reading × least count)
formulas.use: Find an observed screw-gauge thickness (main-scale reading and least count in the same length unit; circular-scale reading is a number of divisions).

formulas.formula: Corrected reading = observed reading − zero error (positive zero error); corrected reading = observed reading + zero error (negative zero error)
formulas.use: Correct an instrument reading for zero error (all readings and zero error in the same length unit).

formulas.formula: Volume of solid = final liquid reading − initial liquid reading
formulas.use: Find a solid’s volume by displacement in a measuring cylinder (all volumes in the same unit, such as cm³ or mL).

formulas.formula: 1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1 g cm⁻³ = 1000 kg m⁻³
formulas.use: Convert volume units or convert density from g cm⁻³ to kg m⁻³ (volume in cm³ or mL; density in the stated units).

fullMarks: For a definition or law, write the complete statement clearly; for a comparison question, name both quantities or units being compared.
In SI-unit questions, write each physical quantity with its correct unit name and symbol; keep symbols in the correct case, such as K, A, m and kg.
For scientific notation, show how the decimal point is moved and use a positive exponent when it moves left and a negative exponent when it moves right.
For addition or subtraction in scientific notation, first make the powers of 10 equal; then combine the coefficients and write the answer in normalized scientific notation.
For instrument numericals, show the scale reading, least count, formula, substitution and final answer with a unit; apply the zero-error correction if the question gives one.
For a metre-scale measurement, avoid parallax by placing the eye directly above the reading; if the zero end is worn, start from a clear mark and subtract that starting reading.
For a displacement measurement, record both initial and final liquid readings and state that the difference is the solid’s volume.
For significant-figure questions, count leading, captive and trailing zeros by the stated rules; keep the required significant figures and unit in the final answer.
mistakes: Writing a number without a unit: include the unit in the final answer because a measurement has both a number and a unit.
Treating leading zeros as significant: zeros before the first non-zero digit do not count, so 0.0045 has two significant figures.
Adding or subtracting scientific-notation values with different exponents directly: first rewrite them with the same power of 10.
Forgetting that the Vernier or circular-scale reading is multiplied by the least count: show the multiplication before adding the main-scale reading.
Using the wrong sign for zero-error correction: subtract a positive zero error and add a negative zero error as instructed for the instrument.
Reading a scale from an angle or reading a water meniscus from above: keep the eye level with the reading and directly in front of the scale.
Using incorrect symbol case or spacing, such as writing K as k or placing a space between a prefix and unit: write symbols correctly and keep a prefix attached to its unit.

shortTheory.question: What is measurement? Name its two parts.
shortTheory.answer: A measurement is a process of comparison of an unknown quantity with a widely accepted standard quantity. A measurement consists of two parts, a number and a unit.

shortTheory.question: Why do we need a standard unit for measurements?
shortTheory.answer: This measurement may result in confusion as the measurement of different people may differ from each other because of different sizes of their hands, arms or steps. To avoid such confusion, there is a need of a standard so that measurement by any person may result the same.

shortTheory.question: Write the name of 3 base quantities and 3 derived quantities.
shortTheory.answer: Base quantities include length, mass and time. Derived quantities include speed, area and volume.

shortTheory.question: Write the name and symbols of all SI base units.
shortTheory.answer: Length — metre (m); mass — kilogram (kg); time — second (s); temperature — kelvin (K); electric current — ampere (A); intensity of light — candela (cd); amount of substance — mole (mol).

shortTheory.question: Why prefix is used? Name three sub-multiple and three multiple prefixes with their symbols.
shortTheory.answer: The use of prefixes makes large and small quantities simple to write down. Three sub-multiple prefixes are milli (m), centi (c) and micro (μ). Three multiple prefixes are kilo (k), mega (M) and giga (G).

shortTheory.question: Can a non-physical quantity be measured? If yes, then how?
shortTheory.answer: Other quantities quoted above such as love, affection, fear, wisdom, and beauty cannot be measured using tools and instruments. They often pertain to the perception or interpretation of the observer. They can be described or qualitatively or compared using some pre-determined criteria, indices or through survey techniques.

explain.title: Scalars
explain.body: A scalar is that physical quantity which can be described completely by its magnitude only. Magnitude includes a number and an appropriate unit. Distance, length, time, speed, energy and temperature are examples of scalars. Scalar quantities can be added up like numbers.

explain.title: Vectors
explain.body: A vector is that physical quantity which needs magnitude as well as direction to describe it completely. Displacement, velocity, acceleration, weight and force are examples of vectors. Their directions must be considered when vectors are added.

explain.title: Drawing a vector
explain.body: A vector is drawn as a straight line with an arrowhead at one end. The length represents magnitude according to a suitable scale, while the arrow indicates direction. To specify direction, use reference axes and measure the angle from the appropriate axis.

explain.title: Adding vectors graphically

writtenQuestions.text: Describe different types of motion. Also give examples.
modelAnswer: There are three general types of motion: translatory, rotatory and vibratory.
If every particle of a body moves uniformly in the same direction, it is called translatory motion; the motion of a train or a car is an example.
Translatory motion can be linear, random or circular: a freely falling body is linear, a bee moving along an irregular path is random, and a Ferris wheel is circular.
If each point of a body moves around a fixed point (axis), the motion is called rotatory motion; an electric fan or a top is an example.
When a body repeats its to and fro motion about a fixed position, the motion is called vibratory motion; a swing is an example.

explain.title: The three general types
explain.body: Generally, there are three types of motion of bodies: translatory motion, rotatory motion, and vibratory motion.

explain.title: Translatory motion and its types
explain.body: “If the motion of a body is such that every particle of the body moves uniformly in the same direction, it is called translatory motion.” It can be linear (along a straight line), random (along an irregular path), or circular (along a circle).

explain.title: Rotatory motion
explain.body: “If each point of a body moves around a fixed point (axis), the motion of this body is called rotatory motion.” An electric fan and a top are examples.

explain.title: Vibratory motion
explain.body: “When a body repeats its to and fro motion about a fixed position, the motion is called vibratory motion.” A swing is an example.

mistakes: Do not confuse circular motion along a circular path with rotatory motion around a fixed axis; use the movement described in the question.
Do not call every back-and-forth movement rotatory: repeated to-and-fro motion about a fixed position is vibratory motion.
Do not define random motion as simply changing direction; the textbook definition is movement along an irregular path.
When asked for types of motion, include examples as well as the names.

recap.question: A passenger is sitting in a moving train. Is the passenger at rest or in motion compared with someone standing on the platform?

writtenQuestions.text: Distance and displacement may or may not be equal in magnitude. Explain this statement.
modelAnswer: Distance is the length of the actual path followed by the object.
Displacement is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions.
If the object moves in a straight line in one direction, distance and the magnitude of displacement are equal.
If the path is curved or the object changes direction, distance is greater than the magnitude of displacement.

writtenQuestions.text: Explain the difference between distance and displacement.
modelAnswer: Distance is the length of actual path of the motion.
Displacement is a vector quantity whose magnitude is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions of the motion.
Its direction is from the initial position to the final position.
Distance is a scalar quantity whereas displacement is a vector quantity.

explain.title: Distance measures the route
explain.body: The distance is the length of actual path of the motion. It is a scalar quantity, so it has magnitude but no direction.

explain.title: Displacement measures the change in position
explain.body: The displacement of an object is a vector quantity whose magnitude is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions of the motion and its direction is from the initial position to the final position.

explain.title: They can have different magnitudes
explain.body: If an object follows a curved path or turns, its actual path is longer than the straight-line displacement. If it travels straight in one direction, the distance and the magnitude of displacement are equal.

explain.title: Speed
explain.body: We are often interested to know how fast a body is moving. For this purpose, we have to find the distance covered in unit time which is known as speed. If a body covers a distance S in time t, its speed v will be written as: Speed = Distance/Time  v = S/t or S = vt. The speed is a scalar quantity.

explain.title: Average and instantaneous speed
explain.body: The speed of a vehicle that is shown by its speedometer at any instant is called instantaneous speed. Practically we make use of the average speed. It is defined as: Average speed = (Total distance covered)/(Total time taken) or v_av = S/t

explain.title: Velocity
explain.body: The net displacement of a body in unit time is called velocity. Average velocity = Displacement/Time or vector v_av = vector d/t. Velocity is a vector quantity. The direction of velocity vector v is the same as that of displacement vector d.

explain.title: Uniform and non-uniform velocity
explain.body: The velocity is said to be uniform if the speed and direction of a moving body does not change. If the speed or direction or both of them change, it is known as variable velocity or non-uniform velocity.

mistakes: Using distance instead of displacement when finding average velocity.
Forgetting that velocity includes direction, while speed does not.
Assuming that constant speed always means constant velocity; direction may still change.
Reversing the speed formula when finding time; use t = S/v.
Leaving out units from numerical answers.

explain.title: What acceleration means
explain.body: Acceleration is defined as the time rate of change of velocity. In other words, it tells how quickly velocity changes.

explain.title: Positive and negative acceleration
explain.body: The acceleration is positive if the velocity is increasing and it is negative if the velocity is decreasing. Negative acceleration is also called deceleration or retardation.

explain.title: Acceleration has direction
explain.body: Acceleration is a vector quantity like velocity, but the direction of acceleration is that of change of velocity. A change in velocity can occur in magnitude, direction, or both.

explain.title: Average acceleration
explain.body: If a body is moving with an initial velocity v_i and after some time t its velocity changes to v_f, the change in velocity is Δv = v_f − v_i that occurs in time t. In this case, rate of change of velocity i.e., acceleration will be average acceleration. Use a_av = (v_f − v_i)/t, and write the SI unit as m s⁻².

explain.title: Uniform and non-uniform acceleration
explain.body: If time rate of change of velocity is constant, the acceleration is said to be uniform. If anyone of the magnitude or direction or both of them changes it is called variable or non-uniform acceleration.

mistakes: Using km h⁻¹ directly in an equation when the other values are in SI units; convert it to m s⁻¹ first.
Reversing the subtraction in v_f − v_i, which can give the wrong sign.
Leaving out the minus sign when a body is slowing down.
Writing m s⁻¹ instead of the acceleration unit m s⁻².
Using v_f = v_i + at without checking that acceleration is constant.

steps.why: The independent variable is time, so it belongs on the x-axis; distance is plotted on the y-axis.

steps.text: Plot all pairs of values of time and distance by marking points on the graph paper.

steps.why: The points form a straight line, showing equal distances in equal time intervals and hence uniform speed.

example.question:

explain.title: What a graph shows
explain.body: A graph is a pictorial diagram in the form of a straight line or a curve which shows the relationship between two physical quantities. Time is usually the independent quantity on the x-axis, and the dependent quantity is on the y-axis.

explain.title: Distance-time graph
explain.body: Distance-time graph shows the relation between distance S and time t taken by a moving body. A straight rising line shows uniform speed because the car covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.

explain.title: Curved distance-time graphs
explain.body: An upward-curving graph shows that speed is increasing. A graph that curves downwards and becomes flatter shows that the distance travelled in the same time interval is decreasing, so speed is decreasing.

explain.title: Horizontal distance-time graph
explain.body: If the graph is horizontal, distance does not change with time. The body is at rest.

mistakes: Putting time on the y-axis instead of the x-axis.
Forgetting to choose and label a suitable scale on both axes.
Treating every curved graph as uniform motion; a curved distance-time graph shows changing speed.
Calling a horizontal distance-time graph uniform motion instead of rest.
Leaving out units or the negative sign when calculating the gradient of a falling segment.

yourTurn.question: Prove that the area under speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered by an object.
solution: For a body moving at constant speed, speed = distance/time.
Therefore, distance = speed × time.
The area under its speed-time graph is the area of a rectangle = speed × time.
Hence, the area of the rectangle is equal to the distance covered.
For changing speed, the total area under the graph is the sum of the distances covered in successive time intervals.
Therefore, the area under a speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered by the object.

hints: For constant speed, the area under the graph is a rectangle.

yourTurn.question: Prove that the area under speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered by an object.
solution: For constant speed v during time t, the area under the speed-time graph is the area of a rectangle.
Area of rectangle = v × t.
Distance covered = speed × time = v × t.
For speed increasing uniformly from 0 to v in time t, average speed = (0 + v)/2 = 1/2 v.
Distance covered = average speed × time = 1/2 v × t.
Area of triangle = 1/2 (perpendicular × base) = 1/2 (v × t).
Thus, the area under the speed-time graph up to the time axis is numerically equal to the distance covered by the object.
yourTurn.answer: The area under a speed-time graph up to the time axis is numerically equal to the distance covered by the object.

explain.title: Uniformly increasing speed makes a triangle
explain.body: When speed rises uniformly from zero to v in time t, the graph forms a triangle. Its area is 1/2 × v × t. The average speed is 1/2 v, so distance is also 1/2 v × t.

explain.body: The area under the speed-time graph up to the time axis is numerically equal to the distance covered by the object.

explain.title: The equations of motion
explain.body: Your textbook gives these three equations: v_f = v_i + at; S = v_i t + 1/2 at²; 2aS = v_f² − v_i². Choose the equation that contains the quantities you know and the one you need to find.

explain.title: Assumptions
explain.body: Your textbook states: “Motion is always considered along a straight line”; “Only the magnitudes of vector quantities are used”; and “Acceleration is assumed to be uniform.” Make sure the situation fits these assumptions when using the equations.

explain.title: Direction and signs
explain.body: Your textbook states: “The direction of initial velocity is taken as positive. Other quantities which are in the direction of initial velocity are taken as positive. The quantities in the direction opposite to the initial velocity are taken as negative.” For a dropped object, choose a consistent direction for the calculation and give gravity the matching sign.

modelAnswer: Since freely falling bodies move vertically downwards in a straight line with uniform acceleration g, the three equations of motion can be applied.
Replace acceleration a by gravitational acceleration g in the equations of motion:
v_f = v_i + gt
S = v_i t + ½gt²
2gS = v_f² − v_i²
Take g positive downward; quantities opposite to the acceleration are negative.
For a body released from a height, vᵢ = 0.
For a body thrown vertically upward, g is negative and v_f = 0 at the highest point.

steps.why: Substituting the values gives the time to reach the highest point.
steps.text: Putting the values, t = (0 − 30 m s⁻¹)/−10 m s⁻² = 3 s

steps.why: The third equation connects the two velocities with the displacement without needing time.
steps.text: Now from the third equation of motion: 2gS = v_f² − vᵢ²

steps.why: Rearrange the equation to make height the subject, using the negative acceleration for upward motion.
steps.text: S = (v_f² − vᵢ²)/2(−g)

steps.why: Substitution gives the maximum height above the launch point.
steps.text: Putting the values h = (0 − (30)² m² s⁻²)/(2 × 10 m s⁻²) = 45 m

example.question: An arrow is thrown vertically upward with the help of a bow. The velocity of the arrow when it leaves the bow is 30 m s⁻¹. Determine time to reach the highest point? Also, find the maximum height attained by the arrow.
example.answer: Time to reach the highest point = 3 s; maximum height = 45 m.

explain.title: Gravitational acceleration
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “When a body is falling freely under the action of gravity of the Earth, the acceleration acting on it is the gravitational acceleration and is denoted by g.” It also states: “The direction of gravitational acceleration is always downwards. Its value is 9.8 m s⁻², but for convenience we shall use the value of g as 10 m s⁻².”

explain.title: Equations for freely falling bodies
explain.body: The three equations of motion are used with a replaced by g: v_f = v_i + gt; S = v_i t + ½gt²; 2gS = v_f² − v_i². Choose the equation that includes the unknown you need.

explain.title: Choose signs carefully
explain.body: Use g as positive when downward is positive. Quantities in the opposite direction are negative. If a body is released from a height, vᵢ = 0. If it is thrown vertically upward, g is negative and the final velocity at the highest point is zero.

explain.title: Objects fall with the same acceleration
explain.body: Your textbook states: “Acceleration of free fall g is 10 m s⁻² for all objects.” The section also notes that light and heavier objects fall side by side through a vacuum.

mistakes: Using g = +10 m s⁻² for a body thrown upward; in that case use g = −10 m s⁻².
Forgetting that a body released from rest has vᵢ = 0.
Using a non-zero final velocity at the highest point; there v_f = 0.
Giving a velocity without a unit or using the wrong unit; velocity is measured in m s⁻¹ and acceleration in m s⁻².
Forgetting that the stated height for an upward-thrown object may be the rise above its starting point, not its height above the ground.

recap.question: A stone is dropped from rest and falls for 3 s. Take g = 10 m s⁻². What is its final velocity?
recap.answer: t = 3 s; v_f = 30 m s⁻¹ downward.

recap.question: In third equation of motion 2aS + V_i² =
recap.answer: V_f²

solutions.question: An iron bob is dropped from the top of a tower. It reaches the ground in 4 seconds. Find: (a) the height of the tower (b) the velocity of the ball as it strikes the ground.
steps: For freely falling body:
Initial velocity = v_i = 0
Acceleration = g = 10 m s⁻²
Time = t = 4 s
Height (distance) = S = h = ?
Final velocity = v_f = ?
(a) According to second equation of motion,
S = v_i t + 1/2 gt²
Putting the values, h = 0 × 4 s + 1/2 × 10 m s⁻² × (4)² s²
h = 80 m
(b) From the first equation of motion, we have
v_f = v_i + gt
Putting the values, v_f = 0 + 10 m s⁻² × 4s = 40 m s⁻¹

solutions.question: An arrow is thrown vertically upward with the help of a bow. The velocity of the arrow when it leaves the bow is 30 m s⁻¹. Determine time to reach the highest point? Also, find the maximum height attained by the arrow.
steps: Here, acceleration will be taken as negative, for the arrow is thrown vertically upward.
Initial velocity = v_i = 30 m s⁻¹
Final velocity = v_f = 0
Acceleration = g = -10 m s⁻²
Time = t = ?
Height S = h = ?
From first equation of motion:
v_f = v_i + gt
or
t = (v_f − v_i)/−g
Putting the values t = (0 − 30 m s⁻¹)/−10 m s⁻² = 3 s
Now from the third equation of motion:
2gS = v_f² − v_i²
or
S = (v_f² − v_i²)/2(−g)
Putting the values h = (0 − (30)² m² s⁻²)/(2 × 10 m s⁻²) = 45 m

rubric.how: State that it has magnitude only.

rubric.how: State that it has both magnitude and direction.

Examples of vectors are displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and weight.

examTips: Section A tests key facts and graph meanings; revise which graph gradient gives speed, velocity or acceleration, and which graph area gives distance.
Short answers commonly ask for definitions, examples and a brief reason. Include the defining feature, such as direction for a vector.
For graph questions, identify the axes and interpret the gradient or area before giving the answer.
For numericals, write the known quantities, convert to compatible units, state the equation, substitute values with units and give the final answer with its unit.
In motion under gravity, write the chosen positive direction and use the sign of g consistently. Marks are commonly awarded for the equation, substitution, working and final answer.

s = ut + ½at².

example.question: Q2.4. A car passes a green traffic signal while moving with a velocity of 5 m s⁻¹. It then accelerates to 1.5 m s⁻². What is the velocity of car after 5 seconds?

explain.title: Scalars and vectors
explain.body: A scalar has magnitude only. A vector has both magnitude and direction. Distance and speed are scalars; displacement, velocity and acceleration are vectors.

explain.title: Distance and displacement
explain.body: Distance is the total path travelled. Displacement is the change in position in a specified direction. Displacement magnitude cannot be greater than distance.

explain.title: Speed, velocity and acceleration
explain.body: Speed is distance per unit time. Velocity is displacement per unit time. Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time.

explain.title: Motion graphs
explain.body: The gradient of a distance–time graph gives speed; the gradient of a displacement–time graph gives velocity. The gradient of a speed–time graph gives acceleration, and its area gives distance.

explain.title: Equations of motion
explain.body: For constant acceleration, use v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², or v² = u² + 2as. For motion under gravity, use g as the acceleration and keep the chosen direction and signs consistent.

mistakes: Treating distance and displacement as identical even when direction changes.
Calling velocity uniform just because speed is constant; direction must also stay constant.
Reading the gradient of a speed–time graph as distance; distance is the area under that graph.
Forgetting to convert km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ before using SI units in an equation.
Using the wrong sign for gravity or braking acceleration.
Leaving units out of a numerical answer or omitting the direction when it matters.

recap.question: A stone is dropped from rest. What is its initial velocity, and which way is g positive?
recap.answer: For a body dropped from rest, vᵢ = 0 and g = 10 m s⁻² downward.

recap.question: Value of “g” increases with the
recap.answer: Decrease in altitude

solutions.question: Define scalar and vector quantities.
steps: A scalar quantity is a physical quantity which has magnitude only and no direction.
A vector quantity is a physical quantity which has both magnitude and direction.
solutions.answer: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and direction.

solutions.question: Give 5 examples each for scalar and vector quantities.
steps: Examples of scalar quantities: distance, speed, time, mass and temperature.
Examples of vector quantities: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and weight.
solutions.answer: Scalars: distance, speed, time, mass and temperature. Vectors: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and weight.

solutions.question: State head-to-tail rule for addition of vectors.
steps: To add vectors by the head-to-tail rule, place the tail of the second vector at the head of the first vector.
The resultant vector is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the head of the last vector.
solutions.answer: Join the vectors head to tail; the resultant extends from the first tail to the last head.

solutions.question: What are distance- time graph and speed-time graph?
steps: A distance-time graph represents the distance covered by a body with respect to time.
A speed-time graph represents the speed of a body with respect to time.
solutions.answer: A distance-time graph shows distance against time; a speed-time graph shows speed against time.

solutions.question: Falling objects near the Earth have the same constant acceleration. Does this imply that a heavier object will fall faster than a lighter object?
steps: No. The same constant acceleration of falling objects does not mean that a heavier object falls faster than a lighter object.
In the absence of air resistance, all objects near the Earth fall with the same acceleration, regardless of their masses.
solutions.answer: No. Without air resistance, heavy and light objects fall with the same acceleration.

solutions.question: The vector quantities are sometimes written in scalar notation (not bold face). How is the direction indicated?
steps: When a vector is written in scalar notation, its direction is indicated by a plus (+) or minus (−) sign with respect to a chosen reference direction.
solutions.answer: Its direction is indicated by a plus or minus sign relative to a chosen reference direction.

solutions.question: A body is moving with uniform speed. Will its velocity be uniform? Give reason.
steps: No, not necessarily.
Velocity is uniform only when both speed and direction remain constant.
A body moving with uniform speed may change its direction; therefore, its velocity may change.
solutions.answer: Uniform speed does not necessarily mean uniform velocity, because the direction may change.

solutions.question: Is it possible for a body to have acceleration? When moving with: (i) constant velocity (ii) constant speed
steps: (i) A body moving with constant velocity has no acceleration, because its velocity does not change.
(ii) A body moving with constant speed may have acceleration if its direction changes, as in circular motion.
If it moves with constant speed in a straight line without changing direction, its acceleration is zero.
solutions.answer: Constant velocity means zero acceleration; constant speed can have acceleration if direction changes.

solutions.question: Distance and displacement may or may not be equal in magnitude. Explain this statement.
steps: Distance is the total length of the actual path travelled by an object, whereas displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from its initial to its final position in a specified direction.
If an object moves along a straight line in one direction, the magnitude of its distance and displacement are equal.
If an object changes direction or follows a curved path, the magnitude of its distance is greater than the magnitude of its displacement.
solutions.answer: Distance and displacement are equal in magnitude for straight-line motion in one direction; otherwise, distance is greater.

solutions.question: When a bullet is fired, its velocity with which it leaves the barrel is called the muzzle velocity of the gun. The muzzle velocity of one gun with a longer barrel is lesser than that of another gun with a shorter barrel. In which gun is the acceleration of the bullet larger? Explain your answer.
steps: Assume the bullet starts from rest and has uniform acceleration while moving through the barrel.
For motion with uniform acceleration, v² = u² + 2as. Since u = 0, a = v²/(2s).
The gun with the longer barrel produces a lower muzzle velocity, while its barrel length is greater.
Therefore, its value of v²/(2s) is smaller. The bullet's acceleration is larger in the gun with the shorter barrel.
solutions.answer: The bullet's acceleration is larger in the gun with the shorter barrel.

solutions.question: For a complete trip, average velocity was calculated. Its value came out to be positive. Is it possible that its instantaneous velocity at any time during the trip had the negative value? Give justification of your answer.
steps: Yes, it is possible.
A positive average velocity for the complete trip means that the net displacement is in the positive direction.
The object may move in the negative direction during part of the trip and still have a positive net displacement for the complete trip.
Therefore, its instantaneous velocity may be negative at some time during the trip.
solutions.answer: Yes. Instantaneous velocity can be negative during part of a trip even when average velocity for the complete trip is positive.

solutions.question: A ball is thrown vertically upward with velocity v. It returns to the ground in time T. Which of the following graphs correctly represents the motion? Explain your reasoning.
steps: For upward motion, take the upward direction as positive.
The ball has initial velocity +v and constant acceleration −g due to gravity.
Its velocity decreases uniformly with time, becomes zero at the highest point, and then becomes negative as the ball falls.
Thus, the correct velocity–time graph is a straight line with negative slope, starting at +v, crossing the time axis at T/2, and ending at −v at time T.
solutions.answer: The correct velocity–time graph is a straight line from +v at t = 0 to −v at t = T, crossing zero at T/2.

solutions.question: The figure given below shows the distance - time graph for the travel of a cyclist. Find the velocities for the segments a, b and c.
steps: The distance–time graph referred to in the question is not included, so the numerical velocities of segments a, b and c cannot be determined.
The velocity for each segment is found from the slope of that segment of the distance–time graph: velocity = change in distance / change in time.
A steeper segment represents a greater velocity; a horizontal segment represents zero velocity.
solutions.answer: The velocities cannot be calculated without the graph and its scale; each is the slope of its segment.

solutions.question: Is it possible that the velocity of an object is zero at an instant of time, but its acceleration is not zero? If yes, give an example of such a case.
steps: Yes, it is possible for the velocity of an object to be zero at an instant while its acceleration is not zero.
For example, when a ball is thrown vertically upward, its velocity is zero for an instant at the highest point.
At that instant, its acceleration is still g downward due to gravity.
solutions.answer: Yes. At the highest point of a vertically thrown ball, velocity is momentarily zero but acceleration is g downward.

solutions.question: How a vector can be represented graphically? Explain.
steps: A vector is represented graphically by a directed line segment.
The length of the line segment, drawn according to a suitable scale, represents the magnitude of the vector.
The arrowhead shows the direction of the vector.
The vector is labelled with its symbol.
solutions.answer: A vector is shown by a scaled directed line segment: its length represents magnitude and its arrowhead represents direction.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: (a) rest and motion
steps: Rest: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings.
Motion: An object is in motion if its position changes with time relative to its surroundings.
Rest and motion are relative terms; an object may be at rest relative to one body and in motion relative to another.
solutions.answer: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings, and in motion if it does.

solutions.question: Differentiate between: (b) speed and velocity
steps: Speed is the distance covered by an object in unit time.
Velocity is the displacement of an object in unit time in a specified direction.
Speed is a scalar quantity; it has magnitude only.
Velocity is a vector quantity; it has both magnitude and direction.
solutions.answer: Speed is distance per unit time and a scalar; velocity is displacement per unit time in a specified direction and a vector.

solutions.question: Describe different types of motion. Also give examples.
steps: Motion is of three types: translatory motion, rotatory motion and vibratory motion.
In translatory motion, a body moves from one place to another. Its particles move the same distance in the same direction in a given time.

Translatory motion may be linear, circular or random. A car moving along a straight road shows linear motion; a stone tied to a string and whirled shows circular motion; and the motion of gas molecules shows random motion.
In rotatory motion, a body spins about an axis passing through it. The spinning of a fan is an example.
In vibratory motion, a body moves to and fro about its mean position. The motion of a simple pendulum is an example.
solutions.answer: The three types of motion are translatory, rotatory and vibratory motion; examples include a moving car, a spinning fan and a simple pendulum, respectively.

solutions.question: Explain the difference between distance and displacement.
steps: Distance is the length of the actual path covered by a moving body.
Displacement is the shortest distance between the initial and final positions of a body in a specified direction.
Distance is a scalar quantity, whereas displacement is a vector quantity.
Distance is always positive, while displacement may be positive, negative or zero.
The magnitude of displacement is always less than or equal to the distance travelled.
solutions.answer: Distance is the actual path length; displacement is the shortest directed distance from the initial to the final position.

solutions.question: What do gradients of distance-time graph and speed-time graph represent? Explain it by drawing diagrams.
Prove that the area under speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered by an object.
steps: Consider an object moving with uniform speed v for time t.
Distance covered, s = speed × time = vt.
The area under its speed-time graph is the area of a rectangle.
Area = base × height = t × v = vt.
Therefore, the area under the speed-time graph is equal to the distance covered. For a changing speed, the area under the graph gives the total distance covered.
solutions.answer: The area under a speed-time graph represents the distance covered by the object.

solutions.question: How equations of motion can be applied to the bodies moving under the action of gravity?
steps: For a body moving under gravity, the acceleration a in the equations of motion is replaced by the acceleration due to gravity g.
The equations of motion become: v = u + gt; s = ut + ½gt²; v² = u² + 2gs.
These equations apply when downward is taken as the positive direction.
If upward is taken as positive, the acceleration is −g, so g is replaced by −g in the equations.
solutions.answer: For motion under gravity, use the equations of motion with a = g (or a = −g when upward is positive).

solutions.question: Draw the representative lines of the following vectors: (a) A velocity of 400 m s⁻¹ making an angle of 60° with x-axis.
steps: Choose the scale 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹.
Draw the positive x-axis as the reference direction.
From the origin, measure 60° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis and draw a 4 cm line in that direction.
Put an arrowhead at the end and label the line 400 m s⁻¹.
solutions.answer: The representative line is 4 cm long at 60° to the positive x-axis, labelled 400 m s⁻¹, using the scale 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹.

drawn.title: Velocity vector
drawn.description: Draw the representative line 4 cm long, at 60° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Scale: 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹. Add an arrowhead and label it 400 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: Draw the representative lines of the following vectors: (b) A force of 50 N making an angle of 120° with x-axis.
steps: Choose the scale 1 cm = 10 N.
Draw the positive x-axis as the reference direction.
From the origin, measure 120° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis and draw a 5 cm line in that direction.
Put an arrowhead at the end and label the line 50 N.
solutions.answer: The representative line is 5 cm long at 120° to the positive x-axis, labelled 50 N, using the scale 1 cm = 10 N.

drawn.title: Force vector
drawn.description: Draw the representative line 5 cm long, at 120° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Scale: 1 cm = 10 N. Add an arrowhead and label it 50 N.

solutions.question: A car is moving with an average speed of 72 km h⁻¹. How much time will it take to cover a distance of 360 km?
steps: Given: Average speed, v = 72 km h⁻¹ = 20 m s⁻¹; distance, d = 360 km = 360000 m.
Required: Time, t.
Formula: t = d / v.
Substitution: t = 360000 m / 20 m s⁻¹.
Working: t = 18000 s = 5 h.
Result: The car will take 5 h.
solutions.answer: 5 h

solutions.question: A truck starts from rest. It reaches a velocity of 90 km h⁻¹ in 50 seconds. Find its average acceleration.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹; final velocity, v = 90 km h⁻¹ = 25 m s⁻¹; time, t = 50 s.
Required: Average acceleration, a.
Formula: a = (v − u) / t.
Substitution: a = (25 m s⁻¹ − 0 m s⁻¹) / 50 s.
Working: a = 25 / 50 = 0.5 m s⁻².
Result: The average acceleration is 0.5 m s⁻².
solutions.answer: 0.5 m s⁻²

solutions.question: A car passes a green traffic signal while moving with a velocity of 5 m s⁻¹. It then accelerates to 1.5 m s⁻². What is the velocity of car after 5 seconds?
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 5 m s⁻¹; acceleration, a = 1.5 m s⁻²; time, t = 5 s.
Required: Final velocity, v.
Formula: v = u + at.
Substitution: v = 5 m s⁻¹ + (1.5 m s⁻² × 5 s).
Working: v = 5 m s⁻¹ + 7.5 m s⁻¹ = 12.5 m s⁻¹.
Result: The velocity of the car after 5 s is 12.5 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: A motorcycle initially travelling at 18 km h⁻¹ accelerates at constant rate of 2 m s⁻². How far will the motorcycle go in 10 seconds?
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 18 km h⁻¹ = 5 m s⁻¹; acceleration, a = 2 m s⁻²; time, t = 10 s.
Required: Distance travelled, s.
Formula: s = ut + ½at².
Substitution: s = (5 m s⁻¹ × 10 s) + ½(2 m s⁻² × (10 s)²).
Working: s = 50 m + 100 m = 150 m.
Result: The motorcycle will travel 150 m.

solutions.question: A wagon is moving on the road with a velocity of 54 km h⁻¹. Brakes are applied suddenly. The wagon covers a distance of 25 m before stopping. Determine the acceleration of the wagon.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 54 km h⁻¹ = 15 m s⁻¹; final velocity, v = 0 m s⁻¹; distance, s = 25 m.
Required: Acceleration, a.
Formula: v² = u² + 2as.
Substitution: (0 m s⁻¹)² = (15 m s⁻¹)² + 2a(25 m).
Working: 0 = 225 + 50a; therefore, a = −225 / 50 = −4.5 m s⁻².
Result: The acceleration of the wagon is −4.5 m s⁻².

solutions.question: A stone is dropped from a height of 45 m. How long will it take to reach the ground? What will be its velocity just before hitting the ground?
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹; distance fallen, s = 45 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Time taken, t, and final velocity, v.
Formula: s = ut + ½gt²; v = u + gt.
Substitution: 45 m = (0 m s⁻¹ × t) + ½(10 m s⁻² × t²).
Working: 45 = 5t²; t² = 9; therefore, t = 3 s. Then v = 0 + (10 m s⁻² × 3 s) = 30 m s⁻¹.
Result: The stone takes 3 s to reach the ground and its velocity just before hitting the ground is 30 m s⁻¹.
solutions.answer: 3 s, 30 m s⁻¹

solutions.question: A car travels 10 km with an average velocity of 20 m s⁻¹. Then it travels in the same direction through a diversion at an average velocity of 4 m s⁻¹ for the next 0.8 km. Determine the average velocity of the car for the total journey.
steps: Given: First distance, d₁ = 10 km = 10000 m; first average velocity, v₁ = 20 m s⁻¹; second distance, d₂ = 0.8 km = 800 m; second average velocity, v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹.
Required: Average velocity for the total journey, v̄.
Formula: v̄ = total displacement / total time.
Substitution: t₁ = d₁ / v₁ = 10000 m / 20 m s⁻¹ = 500 s; t₂ = d₂ / v₂ = 800 m / 4 m s⁻¹ = 200 s.
Working: Total displacement = 10000 m + 800 m = 10800 m; total time = 500 s + 200 s = 700 s. Therefore, v̄ = 10800 m / 700 s = 15.4 m s⁻¹.
Result: The average velocity of the car for the total journey is 15.4 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: A ball is dropped from the top of a tower. The ball reaches the ground in 5 seconds. Find the height of the tower and the velocity of the ball with which it strikes the ground.
steps: Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m s⁻¹; time, t = 5 s; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻².
Required: Height of the tower, s, and velocity of the ball when it strikes the ground, v.
Formula: s = ut + ½gt²; v = u + gt.
Substitution: s = (0 m s⁻¹ × 5 s) + ½(10 m s⁻² × (5 s)²).
Working: s = 125 m. Also, v = 0 + (10 m s⁻² × 5 s) = 50 m s⁻¹.
Result: The height of the tower is 125 m and the ball strikes the ground with a velocity of 50 m s⁻¹.

solutions.question: A cricket ball is hit so that it travels straight up in the air. An observer notes that it took 3 seconds to reach the highest point. What was the initial velocity of the ball? If the ball was hit 1 m above the ground, how high did it rise from the ground?
steps: Given: Time to reach highest point, t = 3 s; height above ground at which the ball was hit, h₀ = 1 m; acceleration due to gravity, g = 10 m s⁻² downward.
Required: Initial velocity, u; maximum height from the ground, H.
At the highest point, final velocity v = 0.
Using v = u − gt: u = v + gt.
Substitution: u = 0 m s⁻¹ + (10 m s⁻²)(3 s).
Working: u = 30 m s⁻¹.
Using s = ut − ½gt², the height risen above the point of launch is: s = (30 m s⁻¹)(3 s) − ½(10 m s⁻²)(3 s)².
Working: s = 90 m − 45 m = 45 m.
