notes.simple: Think of particles as tiny moving pieces. In a solid they stay close to fixed places, in a liquid they slide past one another, and in a gas they are far apart and move freely.
examples: Solid: its particles vibrate about fixed positions, so it has a definite shape and volume.
Gas: its particles are far apart, so it has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.
steps: Identify how the particles are arranged and move.
Relate their motion and spacing to the forces between them.
Use these features to explain whether the substance has a definite shape or volume.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does a liquid have a definite volume but no definite shape?
notes.checkAnswer: A liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape. Its molecules can slide over one another, so it takes the shape of its container.

notes.title: Temperature, Heat and Internal Energy
notes.answer: Heat is energy transferred from a hotter body to a colder body because of a temperature difference.
notes.explanation: Temperature tells how hot or cold a body is. Heat is energy transferred between bodies because they have different temperatures. A body has internal energy, not heat stored inside it.
notes.simple: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is. Heat is energy moving from a hotter object to a colder one.
examples: A spoon becomes hot when left in hotter water: thermal energy transfers from the water to the spoon.
When you touch a cold surface, energy transfers from your warmer hand to the surface.
steps: Compare the temperatures of the two bodies.
Thermal energy transfers from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.
The energy transferred is called heat.
The sum of the molecules' kinetic and potential energies is the body's internal energy.
notes.checkQuestion: Which way does thermal energy flow when two bodies have different temperatures?
notes.checkAnswer: Thermal energy flows from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.

notes.title: Thermometers and temperature scales
notes.answer: A thermometer measures temperature using a thermometric property that changes with temperature.
notes.explanation: A thermometer measures temperature by using a property that changes when temperature changes. Temperature scales use fixed points, and the Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin readings are related by formulae.
notes.simple: A thermometer uses a measurable change, such as the expansion of mercury, to show temperature. Use the correct formula to convert between temperature scales.
steps: Choose the correct conversion formula.
Substitute the given temperature, keeping the units clear.
Calculate and write the answer with its scale unit.
notes.checkQuestion: Which temperature scale has 273 K as the melting point of ice?
notes.checkAnswer: The Kelvin scale.

notes.title: Sensitivity, Range and Linearity
notes.answer: Sensitivity is the ability to detect small temperature changes; range is the span of temperatures measured; linearity means equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale changes.
notes.explanation: A thermometer is judged by three features: sensitivity (detecting small temperature changes), range (the temperatures it measures), and linearity (equal temperature changes giving equal scale changes). For example, a thermometer marked every 0.1°C is more sensitive than one marked every 1°C. A clinical thermometer has a short range, while a laboratory thermometer can have a longer range. A linear thermometer has evenly spaced scale markings.
notes.simple: Sensitivity tells how small a change a thermometer can notice. Range tells how low and high a temperature it can measure. Linearity means equal temperature changes produce equal scale changes.
examples: A thermometer with 0.1°C divisions is more sensitive than one with 1°C divisions.
A thermometer with evenly spaced scale markings shows linearity.
steps: Check the smallest scale division to compare sensitivity: smaller divisions allow smaller changes to be detected.
Find the lowest and highest temperatures marked to identify the range.
Check whether equal temperature changes correspond to equal scale intervals to identify linearity.
notes.checkQuestion: What does sensitivity tell us about a thermometer?
notes.checkAnswer: Sensitivity is the ability to detect small temperature changes.

notes.title: How a Liquid-in-Glass Thermometer Works
notes.answer: The thin bulb wall helps the liquid respond quickly to temperature changes, while the narrow, uniform bore makes its expansion readable on a linear scale.
notes.explanation: A liquid-in-glass thermometer works because its liquid expands when heated and moves up a narrow, uniform tube. The bulb transfers heat to the liquid; the tube and liquid together make the temperature readable on a scale.
notes.simple: Heat makes the liquid in the bulb expand. It rises in the thin tube, and the scale shows the temperature.
examples: Mercury in a thermometer rises when its temperature increases.
A fine, uniform bore makes a small expansion easier to read on the scale.
steps: The thin wall of the glass bulb allows quick conduction through glass to the liquid from a hot object whose temperature is to be measured.
The liquid responds to the change in temperature and expands.
The uniformity of the narrow tube or bore ensures even expansion of the liquid required to make the linear measuring scale.
Read the liquid level against the scale.
notes.checkQuestion: Why should a liquid-in-glass thermometer have a narrow, uniform tube and a thin-walled bulb?
notes.checkAnswer: The narrow, uniform bore makes the liquid’s expansion correspond evenly to the scale; the thin bulb wall helps heat reach the liquid quickly.

notes.title: Temperature, Heat and Thermometers
notes.answer: Heat flows from the hotter body to the colder body.
notes.explanation: Temperature tells how hot or cold something is. Heat is energy transferred from a warmer object to a cooler one. Thermometers use a property that changes with temperature to measure temperature.
notes.simple: Temperature tells how hot or cold a body is. Heat is energy moving from a hotter body to a colder body.
examples: Heat flows from a hot cup of tea to the cooler air around it.
A liquid-in-glass thermometer uses the change in the liquid’s volume as its thermometric property.
steps: Compare the temperatures of the bodies.
Heat flows from the body at higher temperature to the body at lower temperature.
It continues to flow until they reach the same temperature.
notes.checkQuestion: In which direction does heat flow when two bodies at different temperatures are in contact?
notes.checkAnswer: Heat is energy in transit from a warmer object to a cooler object because of a temperature difference.

notes.title: Magnetic and non-magnetic materials
notes.answer: Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials. Brass, copper, wood, glass and plastic are non-magnetic materials.
notes.explanation: A magnet can attract some materials without touching them. Iron, nickel and cobalt are magnetic materials; brass, copper, wood, glass and plastic are non-magnetic materials. To tell whether an object is itself a magnet or only a magnetic material, test it with a known magnet: repulsion shows that the object is a magnet.
notes.simple: A magnet pulls some materials, such as iron, towards it. It does not pull materials such as wood or plastic.
examples: A paper clip made of iron is attracted to a magnet.
A plastic comb is not attracted to a magnet.
steps: Bring a known magnet close to the object.
If the object repels the magnet, the object is a magnet.
If the object is attracted but does not repel, it is a magnetic material, not a magnet.
notes.checkQuestion: What does repulsion by a known magnet tell you about an object?
notes.checkAnswer: An object that repels a known magnet is a magnet. An object that is only attracted is a magnetic material, not a magnet.

notes.title: Properties of Magnets
notes.answer: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Repulsion between like poles is the real test for identifying a magnet.
notes.explanation: A magnet points north–south when freely suspended. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Attraction alone cannot prove that an object is a magnet: it may be a magnetic material. Repulsion by one pole of a suspended magnet is the real test.
notes.simple: Attraction does not prove an object is a magnet. Repulsion does.
examples: Bring an unknown object near the north pole of a suspended magnet. If it is attracted, it might be a south pole or a magnetic material.
Bring the same end near the south pole. If it is repelled, the object is a magnet; if it is attracted again, it is a magnetic material.
steps: Bring one end of the object near a pole of a suspended magnet.
If it is attracted, test the same end against the other pole.
If attracted by both poles, the object is a magnetic material.
If repelled by the other pole, the object is a magnet.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens when unlike poles are brought near each other?
notes.checkAnswer: Unlike poles attract.

notes.title: Induced Magnetism
notes.answer: The S-pole induces an N-pole at the nail’s near end and an S-pole at its far end. The induced magnetism vanishes when the true magnet is removed.
notes.explanation: A magnet can make a nearby piece of iron or steel act like a magnet. The end nearest the magnet gets the opposite pole, and the far end gets the other pole. When the true magnet is removed, the induced magnetism vanishes.
notes.simple: A magnet can make an iron nail act like a magnet for a while. Take the magnet away, and the nail loses this induced magnetism.
examples: Touch the head of an iron nail to the S-pole of a bar magnet: the nail’s near end becomes N and its far end becomes S.
Remove the bar magnet: the nail’s induced magnetism vanishes.
steps: Place the head of an iron nail against a pole of a bar magnet.
Bring a compass near the pointed end of the nail to check that the nail acts like a magnet.
For an S-pole touching the nail, the near end becomes N and the far end becomes S.
Remove the bar magnet and check the nail again; the induced magnetism vanishes.
notes.checkQuestion: If the S-pole of a bar magnet touches the head of an iron nail, which pole is induced at the nail’s near end?
notes.checkAnswer: The nail has induced magnetism; its near end becomes N and its far end becomes S, and the magnetism vanishes when the bar magnet is removed.

notes.title: Temporary and Permanent Magnets
notes.answer: The chain immediately collapses because the magnetism induced in the iron nails is temporary.
notes.explanation: A temporary magnet acts as a magnet while it is in a magnetic field, but loses its magnetism when that field disappears. A permanent magnet keeps its magnetic properties. Soft iron is commonly used for temporary magnets; steel and special alloys can be used for permanent magnets.
notes.simple: Temporary means the magnetism does not last once the outside magnetic field is gone. Permanent means the magnetism remains.
examples: An iron nail attracted to a magnet can temporarily attract another nail.
Cobalt, alnico and ferrite are examples of materials used for permanent magnets.
steps: Bring an iron nail into contact with a bar magnet.
The nail becomes a temporary magnet and can attract another iron nail.
Remove the chain from the bar magnet.
The iron-nail chain immediately collapses, showing that its induced magnetism was temporary.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to a chain of iron nails when it is pulled away from the bar magnet?
notes.checkAnswer: Temporary magnets lose their magnetic properties when the magnetic field vanishes; permanent magnets retain their magnetic properties.

notes.title: Magnetic Fields Around Magnets
notes.answer: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where another magnetic object experiences a force.
notes.explanation: A magnetic field describes the region around a magnet where another magnetic object can feel a force. Magnetic lines of force show the field’s pattern and direction. Lines close together mean a stronger field; lines farther apart mean a weaker field.
notes.simple: A magnet affects magnetic objects around it, even when they are not touching it. The space where this effect happens is its magnetic field.
examples: A compass needle placed near a magnet turns because it experiences a magnetic force.
In a horseshoe magnet, the field is almost uniform in the gap between its poles, except near the edges.
steps: Look at the pattern of magnetic lines of force around a magnet.
Use the N-pole of a compass needle to find the field direction at a point.
Compare the spacing of the lines: closer lines show a stronger field.
Remember that fields of nearby magnets combine; they can cancel at a neutral point.
notes.checkQuestion: Where is a magnetic field stronger: where its lines are close together or far apart?
notes.checkAnswer: Magnetic field strength is greater where the magnetic lines of force are closer together.

notes.title: Uses of Permanent Magnets
notes.answer: Permanent magnets are used in generators and loudspeakers, as well as in door catchers, refrigerator door strips, flourmills, medical tools for removing iron splinters, and resetting the pointer in a maximum and minimum thermometer.
notes.explanation: Permanent magnets are used in devices and everyday tasks. In an A.C. generator, a rotating coil in the magnetic field of a permanent magnet produces an induced emf. In a loudspeaker, a changing current in the voice coil interacts with the magnet’s field, making the cone vibrate and produce sound.
notes.simple: A permanent magnet can help make electricity in a generator or help make sound in a loudspeaker.
examples: A.C. generator: a coil rotates between the poles of a permanent magnet.
Loudspeaker: the voice coil and attached cone move back and forth.
steps: In an A.C. generator, rotate a coil between the poles of a permanent magnet.
The magnetic field through the coil changes.
An emf is induced between the ends of the coil.
When the ends are connected to an external circuit, alternating current flows.
notes.checkQuestion: What produces the induced emf in an A.C. generator?
notes.checkAnswer: The changing magnetic field through the rotating coil induces an emf.

notes.title: Electromagnets: magnets made by current
notes.answer: The nail or rod becomes a magnet when electric current passes through a coil of wire around it. It is called an electromagnet.
notes.explanation: An electromagnet is made when electric current passes through a coil around an iron object. It acts as a magnet while current flows. Electromagnets are useful because their magnetism can be switched on and off.
notes.simple: A coil carrying current can make an iron nail magnetic. Turn off the current and the nail stops acting as a magnet.
examples: An iron nail inside a current-carrying coil can attract paper clips.
A scrapyard crane uses a large electromagnet to lift iron and steel, then releases them when the current is switched off.
steps: Wind a covered copper wire around an iron nail to make a coil.
Connect the coil to a battery through a switch.
Switch on the current: the nail becomes a magnet and can attract clips.
Switch off the current: the nail no longer remains a magnet.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens in a circuit breaker when the current becomes excessive?
notes.checkAnswer: A circuit breaker uses an electromagnet to attract an armature. If the current is excessive, the armature detaches from the copper strip and breaks the circuit.

notes.title: How magnetic domains make iron magnetic
notes.answer: The domains become more aligned with the external field, and the iron becomes magnetized.
notes.explanation: A magnetic domain is a small region in a ferromagnetic material where many neighbouring atoms act together like a tiny magnet. In unmagnetized iron, domains point in different directions. An external magnetic field makes more domains point in the same direction, so the iron becomes magnetized.
notes.simple: Imagine many tiny magnets inside iron. If they point in different directions, their effects cancel. If they turn to point mostly the same way, the iron acts like a magnet.
examples: Iron can be magnetized because it contains magnetic domains that can align.
Copper does not form magnetic domains, so magnetism cannot be induced into it in the way it can in iron.
steps: In unmagnetized iron, domains point in different directions.
An external magnetic field makes domains parallel or nearly parallel to it grow.
Other domains rotate towards the direction of the external field.
The iron becomes magnetized and has its own north and south poles.
notes.checkQuestion: What happens to the domains in an unmagnetized piece of iron when an external magnetic field is applied?
notes.checkAnswer: Domains whose magnetism is parallel or nearly parallel to the external field grow, and other domains rotate towards the field.

notes.title: Magnetising and demagnetising magnets
notes.answer: Steel can be magnetised by single-touch or double-touch stroking, or by placing it in a solenoid carrying direct current. A magnet can be demagnetised by strong heating, hammering, or slowly withdrawing it from an A.C. solenoid.
notes.explanation: A steel bar can be magnetised by stroking it with a permanent magnet or by placing it inside a solenoid carrying direct current. A magnet can be demagnetised by strong heating, hammering, or slowly moving it out of a solenoid carrying alternating current.
notes.simple: Magnetising lines up the magnetic domains in a steel bar. Heating or hammering disturbs their alignment; A.C. in a solenoid can also demagnetise a magnet as it is slowly withdrawn.
examples: In single-touch stroking, stroke the bar several times in the same direction with the same pole, lifting the magnet at the end of each stroke.
To demagnetise a magnet using A.C., place it inside a long solenoid carrying alternating current and move it out slowly.
steps: For single-touch, stroke the steel bar from one end to the other several times in the same direction with the same pole, lifting the magnet at the far end.
For double-touch, stroke outwards from the centre using the unlike poles of two magnets at the same time.
For solenoid magnetisation, put the steel bar inside the solenoid and pass direct current through it; use the right-hand grip rule to identify its poles.
To demagnetise a magnet, heat it strongly, hammer it, or slowly move it out of a solenoid carrying alternating current.
notes.checkQuestion: How do you find which end of a steel bar is its N-pole when it is inside a current-carrying solenoid?
notes.checkAnswer: Use the right-hand grip rule: curl the fingers in the direction of current in the solenoid; the thumb points towards the bar's N-pole end.

notes.title: How magnets store sound, video and data
notes.answer: Magnetic recording stores information as magnetism in a tape’s coating or in tiny spots on a disk.
notes.explanation: The recording head acts as an electromagnet. In tape recording, its fringe field magnetises the moving tape’s coating. In a hard disk, a small magnetic head writes and reads information by magnetising tiny spots in different directions.
notes.simple: The head changes electrical signals into magnetism on a tape or disk. Later, the stored magnetism can be read back.
examples: A tape stores sound or picture as varying magnetism in its magnetic coating.
A hard disk stores binary digits as magnetised spots.
steps: Varying currents reach the coil in the recording head.
The coil and iron core form an electromagnet.
The fringe field passes through the magnetic coating on the moving tape and induces magnetism.
The tape retains this induced magnetism after it leaves the head.
A hard disk head writes and reads binary digits by magnetising tiny spots in different directions.
notes.checkQuestion: What part of the magnetic field magnetises the coating on a moving tape?
notes.checkAnswer: The fringe field penetrates the magnetic coating and induces magnetism in it.

notes.title: Soft Iron as a Magnetic Shield
notes.answer: A soft iron casing shields a sensitive magnetic device because magnetic flux is established in the soft iron rather than in the device.
notes.explanation: Soft iron has high magnetic permeability, so magnetic flux passes through it more easily than through air. A soft iron casing around a sensitive magnetic device provides an easier path for the flux, so the device is shielded from the external magnetic field.
notes.simple: Soft iron gives magnetic field lines an easier path than air. A soft iron cover can therefore keep much of the external magnetic field away from a sensitive device.
examples: A sensitive magnetic device can be protected by enclosing it in a soft iron casing.
A soft iron core in an electromagnet is easily magnetised when current flows and quickly loses its magnetism when the current stops.
steps: Soft iron has high magnetic permeability.
Its permeability is higher than that of air.
Magnetic flux is established in the soft iron casing rather than the sensitive device.
The device is therefore shielded from the external magnetic field.
notes.checkQuestion: Why does a soft iron casing shield a sensitive magnetic device?
notes.checkAnswer: The magnetic flux is established in the soft iron casing rather than in the device, shielding the device from the external magnetic field.

notes.title: Magnets, magnetic fields and magnetic materials
notes.answer: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or current-carrying conductor where magnetic effects can be observed.
notes.explanation: This exercise text contains Sections A–D only. It includes no Section E, no numerical problems, and no printed numerical answers. The worked example and your-turn questions therefore use the supplied exercise questions rather than invented numerical problems.
notes.simple: A magnet creates a magnetic field around it. Field lines help us show the direction and strength of that field.
examples: A compass placed near a magnet points along the magnetic field at that position.
Soft iron is used to shield a device because it provides a path for magnetic field lines.
steps: Identify the poles and the magnetic material involved.
Use the direction of magnetic field lines to explain how a compass or another magnet behaves.
For a solenoid, use the current direction to determine which end is north and which is south.
When describing a diagram, label poles and show field lines or current directions clearly.
notes.checkQuestion: In which direction do magnetic field lines go outside a magnet?
notes.checkAnswer: Outside a magnet, field lines go from the north pole to the south pole.

notes.title: The scope of physics
notes.answer: Physics is a fundamental science about matter, energy, space, time, and their connections and interactions.
notes.explanation: Physics studies matter, energy, space, time, and how they are connected. It is a basic part of the physical sciences. Its branches study different parts of nature, and some combine physics with other subjects.
notes.simple: Physics helps us understand how things in the universe behave, from tiny particles to stars and galaxies.
examples: Classical mechanics studies motion and forces.
Astrophysics uses physics to study stars and other objects in space.
steps: Identify the topic being studied, such as motion, heat, light, or particles.
Connect it to the part of physics that studies that topic.
If it combines physics with another field, describe it as interdisciplinary.
notes.checkQuestion: Which branch of physics studies the behaviour of particles at atomic and subatomic levels?
notes.checkAnswer: Physics studies matter, energy, space, time, and their relationships and interactions.

notes.title: Branches of Physics
notes.answer: Optics studies the physical aspects of visible light.
notes.explanation: Physics has different branches because each branch studies a particular kind of physical phenomenon. For example, optics studies visible light, while acoustics studies audible sound.
notes.simple: Physics is divided into branches. Each branch focuses on a different part of the physical world.
examples: A prism separating white light into colours is studied in optics.
The properties of an atom’s nucleus are studied in nuclear physics.
steps: Identify the physical phenomenon in the question.
Match it with the branch that studies that phenomenon.
State the branch and, if asked, what it studies.
notes.checkQuestion: Which branch studies the physical aspects of visible light?
notes.checkAnswer: Optics studies visible light; nuclear physics studies the properties of atomic nuclei.

notes.title: Interdisciplinary Nature of Physics
notes.answer: Interdisciplinary physics is the integration and interaction of physics with other fields of study. Its fields include biophysics, medical physics, astrophysics, geophysics, climate physics and computation physics.
notes.explanation: Physics connects with other fields when its principles and methods are used to study questions in those fields. For example, medical physics uses physics for health diagnosis and treatment, while geophysics uses it to study Earth.
notes.simple: Interdisciplinary physics means using physics together with another subject to study or solve a problem.
examples: MRI is an example of medical physics.
Studying earthquakes using physical principles is an example of geophysics.
steps: Identify what is being studied: health, living things, space, Earth, climate, or a complex physical problem.
Match it to the relevant field: medical physics, biophysics, astrophysics, geophysics, climate physics, or computation physics.
Give a relevant example, such as MRI for medical physics or earthquakes for geophysics.
notes.checkQuestion: Which field of physics applies physical principles to health diagnosis and treatment?
notes.checkAnswer: Medical physics.

notes.title: Interdisciplinary Research
notes.answer: Interdisciplinary research combines knowledge and methods from different fields to address complex issues and foster innovation.
notes.explanation: Interdisciplinary research brings together knowledge and methods from different fields of science. This helps scientists solve complex problems, develop new ideas and share knowledge more quickly.
notes.simple: When a problem is too big for one subject, experts from different subjects work together.
examples: Understanding climate change uses knowledge from meteorology, oceanography, physics, chemistry, biology and environmental sciences.
Nanotechnology combines physics, chemistry, material science and engineering.
steps: Identify the complex issue or research goal.
Bring together the relevant fields of knowledge and expertise.
Share findings and methods, and work together on possible solutions.
Use the combined perspectives to develop understanding, solutions or innovations.
notes.checkQuestion: Why can one field of science be insufficient to address a complex issue such as climate change?
notes.checkAnswer: It combines different fields of knowledge to help solve complex problems or develop new ideas.

notes.title: Scientific Method: From Observation to Law
notes.answer: The scientific method uses observations and experiments to test hypotheses, build theories, make predictions, and, after repeated testing, formulate laws.
notes.explanation: The scientific method is a sequence for investigating a problem: observe, suggest a hypothesis, test it, and use the results to develop explanations and predictions. Repeated successful testing may lead to a law, but scientific ideas can still be changed when new evidence appears.
notes.simple: Observe something, suggest an explanation, and test it. Use the evidence to improve the explanation and make predictions.
examples: Observing a shadow leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
If the holes in a row of cardboards are aligned, torchlight passes through; if one cardboard is moved, the light is blocked.
steps: Identify or recognize an issue or a problem.
Gather information through observations of its various aspects.
Propose an explanation or a guess work known as hypothesis.
Perform experiment or collect evidences to test the hypothesis.
Record, organize and analyze gathered data, plotting and interpreting graphs to reach at a conclusion which is called a theory.
Repeated tests of the theory to wide range of similar issues then lead towards the formulation of a law.
notes.checkQuestion: What must be true of a scientific theory for it to be falsifiable?
notes.checkAnswer: A scientific theory must make predictions that can be tested and could potentially be shown to be false.

notes.title: Scientific knowledge in technology and engineering
notes.answer: Physics provides the scientific principles used in technology and engineering.
notes.explanation: Physics provides scientific principles used in technology and engineering. Technology uses scientific knowledge to develop methods and techniques. Engineering applies scientific principles and technologies to design and build things for specific needs, while also considering cost and safety.
notes.simple: Science helps us understand how things work. Technology uses that knowledge to make methods, machines or programmes. Engineering uses scientific knowledge and technology to design useful things.
examples: Automobile technology is based on the principles of thermodynamics.
A civil engineer designs bridges to withstand strong winds, earthquakes, intense weather conditions and heavy traffic.
steps: Identify the technology, such as automobile, radar or laser technology.
Connect it to the scientific principle stated in your textbook.
For engineering examples, explain what is designed and which need or challenge it addresses.
notes.checkQuestion: Which branch of science plays a vital role in technology and engineering?
notes.checkAnswer: Automobile technology is based on thermodynamics.

notes.title: Nature of Science
notes.answer: Science is the systematic study of the natural world using observation, investigation, and evidence.
notes.explanation: Science studies the natural world through observation, investigation, and evidence. Physics is a physical science concerned with matter, energy, and their interactions. Scientific ideas are tested: a hypothesis is a possible answer to a question, while a theory is a well-supported explanation and a law describes a regular pattern in nature. Scientific knowledge can change when new evidence requires a theory or law to be modified.
notes.simple: Science is a way of learning about nature by asking questions and checking ideas with evidence.
examples: Observing that a plant near a window grows towards the light is an observation.
A prediction might be: if the plant receives more light, it will grow faster.
steps: Ask a question about something you observe.
Suggest a possible answer (hypothesis).
Make a prediction from the hypothesis.
Test the prediction through investigation or an experiment.
Collect and analyse the data.
Use the evidence to support, reject, or modify the hypothesis.
notes.checkQuestion: What is a hypothesis?
notes.checkAnswer: A hypothesis is a possible answer to a question that can be tested.

quiz.stem: What observation helps identify an object as a magnetic material?

Not being attracted indicates a non-magnetic material in the section's test.

quiz.stem: When a bar magnet is suspended horizontally by a string and allowed to come to rest, which direction does it point?

quiz.stem: What is the name of the end of a freely suspended bar magnet that points north?

Incorrect: the south magnetic pole is the end that points south.
Incorrect: the pole is named by the direction it points, not by its colour.

quiz.stem: What happens when the north poles of two magnets are brought near each other?
options: They have no effect on one another.
rationales: Correct: like poles repel, so two north poles repel.
Incorrect: attraction occurs between unlike poles.
Incorrect: the section states that like poles interact by repelling.

quiz.stem: What happens when the south poles of two magnets are brought near each other?
rationales: Correct: two south poles are like poles, and like poles repel.
Incorrect: unlike poles attract; two south poles are alike.
Incorrect: pointing north is a property of a freely suspended magnet, not the interaction of two south poles.

quiz.stem: What happens when a north pole is brought near a south pole?
options: They have no effect on one another.
rationales: Correct: unlike poles attract.
Incorrect: repulsion occurs between like poles.
Incorrect: the section states that unlike poles attract.
Incorrect: bringing unlike poles together does not change either pole into a north pole.

quiz.stem: Which observation is the real test for identifying an object as a magnet?
options: Attraction by either pole of a suspended magnet
Repulsion by one pole of a suspended magnet
rationales: Incorrect: a magnetic material can also be attracted, so attraction alone is not a sure test.
Correct: repulsion by a like pole confirms that the object is a magnet.
Incorrect: colour does not identify a magnet.
Incorrect: weight does not identify a magnet.

quiz.stem: An unknown object is attracted to both ends of a suspended bar magnet. What can you conclude?
options: It is a magnetic material, not a magnet.
rationales: Correct: attraction by both poles indicates a magnetic material rather than a magnet.
Incorrect: attraction alone cannot prove that the object is a magnet.
Incorrect: the observation does not identify the object as a south pole.
Incorrect: testing it against both poles gives a conclusion.

quiz.stem: What happens when a bar magnet is broken into two pieces?

One piece has only a north pole and the other only a south pole.
Only the larger piece remains magnetic.

Incorrect: the section says isolated north and south poles cannot be obtained by breaking a magnet.
Incorrect: both pieces have two poles, regardless of their size.
Incorrect: each piece remains a complete magnet.

quiz.stem: An S-pole is brought into contact with one end of an iron nail. Which statement describes the induced poles?
options: The nail’s near end becomes a pole opposite to the magnet’s touching pole.
The nail’s near end becomes the same pole as the magnet’s touching pole.
Both ends of the nail become north poles.
The nail cannot affect a compass.
rationales: This is correct because the end of the iron nearest the S-pole is induced as N.
This is wrong because the near end acquires the opposite pole, not the same pole.
This is wrong because the two ends become opposite poles, not both north poles.
This is wrong because the magnetised nail can affect a nearby compass.

quiz.stem: What happens to the induced magnetism of an iron nail when the true magnet is removed?
options: The nail changes into a non-magnetic material.
rationales: This is wrong because the section states that induced magnetism vanishes when the true magnet is removed.
This is correct because the nail’s magnetism is induced by the nearby true magnet.
This is wrong because the nail remains iron; it does not change into another material.
This is wrong because removing the magnet from the nail does not mean the bar magnet is demagnetised.

quiz.stem: What is it called when magnetism is produced in a magnetic material by a nearby true magnet?
rationales: This is not the best choice here because the section names the effect as induced magnetism.
This is correct because the material acquires magnetism under the influence of a true magnet.
This is wrong because demagnetization means the loss of magnetism.
This is wrong because magnetic shielding is the protection of a region from an external magnetic field.

quiz.stem: Which material from the list can be made a magnet by induction in the activity?
rationales: This is correct because the activity uses an iron nail to demonstrate induced magnetism.
This is wrong because wood is not the magnetic material used in the activity.
This is wrong because paper is not the magnetic material used in the activity.
This is wrong because glass is not the magnetic material used in the activity.

quiz.stem: Which method follows the section’s activity for checking whether an iron nail has become a magnet?
options: Bring a compass near the nail and observe the needle.
Heat the nail until it glows.
rationales: This is correct because the activity checks the nail’s magnetic effect by observing a nearby compass needle.
This is wrong because heating the nail is not the test used in the activity.
This is wrong because placing the nail in water does not test its magnetic effect.
This is wrong because measuring length gives no information about magnetism.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes a temporary magnet?
options: It loses its magnetic properties when the external magnetic field vanishes.
It keeps its magnetic properties forever.

It can only be made by placing steel in a magnetic field.
rationales: Correct: a temporary magnet loses its magnetic properties when the magnetic field vanishes.
This describes a permanent magnet, not a temporary magnet.

quiz.stem: Which material is usually used to make temporary magnets?
rationales: Correct: soft iron is usually used to make temporary magnets.
Alnico is an example of a permanent magnetic material.
Cobalt is an example of a permanent magnetic material.
Ferrite is an example of a permanent magnetic material.

quiz.stem: Which item from the list can easily be made into a temporary magnet?
rationales: Correct: paper clips are commonly made of iron and can easily be made temporary magnets.
Ferrite is a type of permanent magnetic material.
Alnico is a type of permanent magnetic material.
Cobalt is an example of a permanent magnetic material.

quiz.stem: Why can one iron nail in the activity attract another iron nail?
options: The nails have become permanent magnets.
The nails have become temporary magnets by induction.
The nails have melted and joined together.
The bar magnet has lost all its magnetism.
rationales: The activity shows that the magnetism induced in the iron nails is temporary, not permanent.
Correct: the upper iron nail becomes a temporary magnet and attracts the next nail.
The nails remain separate; melting does not happen in this activity.

quiz.stem: What is observed when the chain of iron nails is removed from the bar magnet?
options: The chain remains attached to the bar magnet forever.
The chain becomes longer by itself.

The chain is removed from the bar magnet, so it cannot remain attached to it.

quiz.stem: What happens to the chain of steel nails when it is removed from the bar magnet?
options: They remain attached to each other for some time.
They immediately collapse in every case.
They lose their magnetic properties before they touch the magnet.

The immediate collapse is the observation for iron nails, not steel nails.
Steel does not become soft iron in the activity.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes a magnetic field?
options: The region where a magnetic object can experience a force
The space inside a magnet only
The path followed by an electric current
rationales: This is correct because a magnetic field is the region around a magnet where another magnetic object experiences a force.

This is incorrect because a current path does not define a magnetic field.

quiz.stem: What does a magnetic line of force represent in the field-pattern method?
options: A line joining the two poles inside a magnet only
A line that shows the path of a magnetic compass needle
A line along which iron filings cannot move
A line that always points towards the south pole of Earth
rationales: This is incorrect because the lines describe the field pattern around the magnet, not only a path inside it.
This is correct because a compass needle moves along the magnetic lines of force.
This is incorrect because iron filings arrange themselves to show the field pattern.

quiz.stem: How is the direction of the magnetic field at a point identified?
options: By the direction of the compass needle’s N-pole

The magnet has no poles at that point
The field is strongest at that point

Water is given as a diamagnetic material.

The domains become aligned opposite to the external field.

Iron remains ferromagnetic; it is the domain orientations that explain its unmagnetized state.

quiz.stem: Which procedure describes the single-touch method of magnetising a steel bar?

Stroke it back and forth with alternating poles without lifting the magnet.
Heat it strongly while stroking it.
Place it in a solenoid carrying alternating current.

quiz.stem: Which current is passed through the solenoid to magnetise the steel bar?

rationales: This is correct: the section says direct current through the solenoid magnetises the steel bar.
This is incorrect because alternating current in a solenoid is described as a way to demagnetise a magnet.
This is incorrect because a current is needed to magnetise the bar by this method.
This is incorrect because the method specifies direct current, not an intermittent current.

Curl the left-hand fingers in the direction of current; the thumb points to the S-pole end.
Point the right-hand thumb in the direction of current; the fingers show the N-pole end.

written.text:
(a) Derive third equation of motion with the help of speed-time graph.
(b) A train moves with a uniform velocity of 36 km h⁻¹ for 10 s. Find the distance travelled by it.
modelAnswer: (a) Let the initial speed be u, the final speed be v, the time be t, the acceleration be a, and the displacement be s.
From the speed-time graph, displacement equals the area under the graph: s = ut + 1/2(v − u)t = 1/2(u + v)t.
From the first equation of motion, v = u + at, so t = (v − u)/a.
Substitute for t: s = 1/2(u + v)(v − u)/a = (v² − u²)/(2a).
Therefore, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u².
Hence, v² = u² + 2as.
(b) Given: v = 36 km h⁻¹ = 10 m s⁻¹, t = 10 s.
Formula: s = vt.
Substitution: s = (10 m s⁻¹)(10 s).
written.followUp: Use a speed-time graph to derive the second equation of motion, s = ut + ½at².

written.text:
(a) Derive the third Equation of Motion with the help of Speed-Time graph.
(b) A cyclist completes half round of a circular track of radius 318 m in 1.5 minutes. Find its speed and velocity.
modelAnswer: (a) Displacement is the area under the speed-time graph, which is a trapezium: s = ½(u + v)t.
From the first equation of motion, v = u + at, so t = (v − u)/a.
Substitute for t: s = ½(u + v)(v − u)/a.
Therefore, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u².
Hence, v² = u² + 2as.
(b) Given: radius r = 318 m; time t = 1.5 min = 90 s.
Distance travelled in half a round = πr = 3.14 × 318 m = 998.52 m.
Speed = distance ÷ time = 998.52 m ÷ 90 s = 11.1 m/s.
Displacement = diameter = 2r = 2 × 318 m = 636 m.
Average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 636 m ÷ 90 s = 7.07 m/s, along the diameter towards the opposite point.
Speed = 11.1 m/s; average velocity = 7.07 m/s along the diameter.
Speed is the distance travelled per unit time; average velocity is the displacement per unit time in the displacement’s direction.

modelAnswer: (a) Draw a speed-time graph with time on the horizontal axis and speed on the vertical axis.
Mark A at (0, u) and B at (t, v), where u is the initial speed and v is the speed after time t.
The gradient of the graph gives acceleration: a = (v − u)/t.
Rearranging: at = v − u.
Therefore, v = u + at.
(b) Given: u = 0 m/s, t = 5 s, g = 9.8 m/s².
Height: s = ut + ½gt².
Velocity on striking the ground: v = u + gt.
v = 0 m/s + (9.8 m/s²)(5 s) = 49 m/s downward.

modelAnswer: (a) For an isolated system, if no external force acts on it, its total momentum remains constant.
During an interaction between two bodies, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite: F1 = -F2.
Since force is the rate of change of momentum, the changes in the bodies’ momenta are equal and opposite.
Therefore, the total momentum before interaction equals the total momentum after interaction: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2.
(b) Given: F = 100 N, m = 50 kg
Formula: a = F/m
Substitution: a = 100 N / 50 kg

written.text:
(a) Determine a force from its perpendicular components.
(b) Find the Perpendicular Components of a Force of 50 N making an angle of 30° with x-axis.
modelAnswer: (a) Let the perpendicular force components be Fx and Fy.
The resultant force R is the diagonal of the right-angled triangle formed by the components.
By Pythagoras' theorem, R^2 = Fx^2 + Fy^2.
Therefore, the magnitude is R = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2).
If θ is measured from Fx, its direction is given by tan θ = Fy/Fx, so θ = tan^-1(Fy/Fx).
(b) Given: F = 50 N, θ = 30° to the x-axis.
Horizontal component: Fx = F cos θ = (50 N) cos 30° = 43.3 N.
Vertical component: Fy = F sin θ = (50 N) sin 30° = 25 N.
The perpendicular components are 43.3 N along the x-axis and 25 N along the y-axis.

written.text:
(a) Define Resolution of forces. How can a force F be resolved into its perpendicular components?
(b) A force is acting on a body making an angle of 30° with the horizontal. The horizontal component of the force is 20 N. Find the force
modelAnswer: (a) Resolution of forces is the process of splitting a force into components along specified directions, whose combined effect is the same as that of the original force.
For a force F making an angle θ with the horizontal, the perpendicular components are horizontal and vertical.
Horizontal component: Fx = F cos θ
Vertical component: Fy = F sin θ
(b) Given: horizontal component F_x = 20 N, angle theta = 30 degrees
Formula: F_x = F*cos(theta)
Rearranging: F = F_x/cos(theta)
Substitution: F = 20/cos(30) N = 23.1 N
Answer: The force is approximately 23.1 N.

written.text:
(a) What is meant by kinetic energy? Derive its equation.
(b) Calculate the power of a pump which can lift 200 kg of water through a height of 6 m in 10 seconds.
modelAnswer: (a) Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
The work done to bring a body from rest to speed v is its kinetic energy.
W = Fs and F = ma, so W = mas.
For a body starting from rest, v² = u² + 2as and u = 0; therefore, s = v²/(2a).
W = ma × v²/(2a) = 1/2mv².
Therefore, kinetic energy, KE = 1/2mv².
(b) Given: m = 200 kg, h = 6 m, t = 10 s and g = 10 m s⁻².
Work done in lifting the water: W = mgh.
Power: P = W/t = mgh/t.
Substituting: P = (200 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 6 m)/(10 s) = 1200 W.
The power of the pump is 1200 W.

(a) State the law of conservation of energy. Explain it with the help of an example of a body falling from certain height in terms of its potential energy and kinetic energy.
(b) A motor boat moves at a steady speed of 4ms⁻¹. Water resistance acting on it is 4000N. Calculate the power of its engine.
modelAnswer: (a) The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form into another.
At a certain height, a body has maximum potential energy and zero kinetic energy if it is at rest.
As the body falls, its potential energy decreases and is converted into kinetic energy, which increases.
Just before reaching the ground, its kinetic energy is maximum and its potential energy is minimum; the total mechanical energy remains constant if air resistance is neglected.
(b) Given: v = 4 m s⁻¹, water resistance = 4000 N.
Since the boat moves at steady speed, the engine force balances the water resistance: F = 4000 N.
Power, P = Fv.
The power of the engine is 16000 W (16 kW).

modelAnswer: (a) Consider a body of height h and cross-sectional area A immersed in a liquid of density ρ.
Let P₁ and P₂ be the pressures on its upper and lower surfaces, respectively.
Pressure difference, P₂ − P₁ = ρgh
Upthrust, F = (P₂ − P₁)A = ρghA
Volume of displaced liquid, V = Ah
Therefore, upthrust of liquid, F = ρgV
(b) Given: ρ = 1.3 kg m⁻³; room dimensions = 8 m × 5 m × 4 m.
Volume of room: V = 8 m × 5 m × 4 m = 160 m³.
Formula: m = ρV.
Substitution: m = 1.3 kg m⁻³ × 160 m³ = 208 kg.
Mass of air in the room = 208 kg.

written.text:
(a) Explain the working process of hydraulic press.
(b) A wooden block measuring 40cm × 10cm × 5cm has a mass 850g. Find the density of wood.
modelAnswer: (a) A hydraulic press works on Pascal’s principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions.
It consists of two pistons of different cross-sectional areas connected by a pipe containing an enclosed liquid.
A force F1 on the smaller piston of area A1 produces pressure P = F1/A1 in the liquid.
The same pressure acts on the larger piston, so F2/A2 = F1/A1.
Because A2 > A1, F2 > F1; the larger force can lift or press a heavy load.
(b) Given: m = 850 g = 0.850 kg.
Dimensions: 40 cm = 0.40 m, 10 cm = 0.10 m, 5 cm = 0.05 m.
Formula: density, ρ = m / V.
Substitution: ρ = 0.850 kg / 0.002 m³ = 425 kg m⁻³.
Answer: the density of the wood is 425 kg m⁻³.

written.text:
(a) Explain Celsius scale and Fahrenheit scale with the figures.
(b) Temperature of water in a beaker is 80°C. What is its value in Fahrenheit scale?
modelAnswer: (a) The Celsius scale has two fixed points: the ice point is 0°C and the steam point is 100°C.
The interval between these points is divided into 100 equal divisions.
Figure (Celsius): 100°C — steam point; 100 equal divisions; 0°C — ice point.
The Fahrenheit scale has two fixed points: the ice point is 32°F and the steam point is 212°F.
The interval between these points is divided into 180 equal divisions.
Figure (Fahrenheit): 212°F — steam point; 180 equal divisions; 32°F — ice point.
(b) Given: C = 80°C.
Formula: F = (9/5)C + 32.
Substitution: F = (9/5)(80) + 32.
Calculation: F = 144 + 32.
Therefore, F = 176°F.
written.followUp: State the fixed points and number of divisions on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales.

mcqs.stem: A magnetic compass is placed around a bar magnet at four points as shown in figure below. Which diagram would indicate the correct directions of the field?

Diagram (b): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point left above, left at the left, left at the right and right below.
Diagram (c): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point right above, left at the left, left at the right and right below.
Diagram (d): horizontal bar magnet with N on the left and S on the right; arrows point left above, left at the left, right at the right and left below.
rationales: In diagram (a), the field direction to the right of the south pole and below the magnet is incorrect.
In diagram (b), the arrows above the magnet and to its left do not follow the field from north to south outside the magnet.
In diagram (c), the arrows correctly show the external field emerging from the north pole and entering the south pole.
In diagram (d), the arrows above and to the right of the magnet point in incorrect directions.

rationales: With the north pole stroking outward toward A and the south pole stroking outward toward B, the resulting poles are N at A and S at B.
This reversed polarity would result if the stroking magnets were oriented the other way around.
A single steel rod magnetised by this method has opposite poles at its ends, not two north poles with a south pole in the middle.

written.text:
(a) What is the scope of Physics in everyday life? Give some examples.
(b) Q9.1. What are the main branches of Physics? State briefly.
modelAnswer: (a) Physics has a wide scope because it explains matter, energy and their interactions in the natural world.
It helps explain everyday motion, such as the movement of objects.
It also explains heat and other familiar physical phenomena.
For example, a swinging pendulum is a motion whose oscillations are described using a time interval.
(b) Mechanics: It is a study of motion and the physical effects which influence motion.
Heat and thermodynamics: It deal with the thermal energy possessed by the materials and it is used when it flows from one body to another.
Acoustics: It deals with the nature and physical aspects of audible sound energy.
Optics: It deal with the physical aspects of visible light.
Electromagnetism: It is the study of electromagnetic phenomenon and mutual relationship between electric current and magnetic field.
Quantum Mechanics: It explains the behaviour of particles at the atomic and subatomic level.

Relativistic Mechanics: It explains how space and time are not absolute quantities but related to observer. It describes the relationship between them and how they are influenced by gravity and speed.
Nuclear Physics: It is the study of the properties of nuclei of the atoms.
Particle Physics: It is the study of subatomic particles and elementary particles which are basic building blocks of matter.
Astronomy: It is study of distribution of celestial bodies like planets, stars and galaxies.
Cosmology: It explores the large structure and evolution of the universe.
Solid State Physics: It is the study of some specific properties of matter in solid form.

written.text:
(a) Is the theory of science an ultimate truth? Describe briefly.
(b) What is scientific method? Describe its main steps with examples.
modelAnswer: (a) No, a scientific theory is not an ultimate truth.
Theories are man-made ideas about the way things work, based on available evidence.
They may be disproved or modified when future advances in science bring fresh facts and new insights about the natural and physical world.
(b) Scientific method is a systematic approach used to search for truth of an issue and problem solving regarding natural and physical world.
First, identify a problem and gather information by observation.
Next, propose a hypothesis and perform an experiment or collect evidence to test it.
Record, organize and analyse the data to reach a conclusion called a theory; repeated tests of the theory over similar issues lead towards a law.
For example, observation of shadows leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
When holes in four cardboards are aligned with a torch, light passes through; when one cardboard is displaced, the light is blocked.
This experiment supports the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line, and repeated testing in different situations may establish a law.

written.text:
(a) Determine a force from its perpendicular components.
(b) The Density of Air is 1.3 Kgm⁻³. Find the Mass of Air in a room measuring 8 m × 5 m × 4 m.
modelAnswer: (a) Let the perpendicular force components be Fx and Fy.
The resultant force R is the diagonal of the right-angled triangle formed by the components.
By Pythagoras' theorem, R^2 = Fx^2 + Fy^2.
Therefore, the magnitude is R = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2).
If θ is measured from Fx, its direction is given by tan θ = Fy/Fx, so θ = tan^-1(Fy/Fx).
(b) Given: ρ = 1.3 kg m⁻³; room dimensions = 8 m × 5 m × 4 m.
Volume of room: V = 8 m × 5 m × 4 m = 160 m³.
Formula: m = ρV.
Substitution: m = 1.3 kg m⁻³ × 160 m³ = 208 kg.
Mass of air in the room = 208 kg.

written.text:
(a) What is thermometer? Also write the characteristics of liquid used in thermometer.
(b) What is scientific method? Describe its main steps with examples.
modelAnswer: (a) A thermometer is an instrument used to measure temperature.
The liquid used in a thermometer should expand uniformly with temperature.
It should have a high boiling point and a low freezing point.
It should be visible and should not wet the glass.
(b) Scientific method is a systematic approach used to search for truth of an issue and problem solving regarding natural and physical world.
First, identify a problem and gather information by observation.
Next, propose a hypothesis and perform an experiment or collect evidence to test it.
Record, organize and analyse the data to reach a conclusion called a theory; repeated tests of the theory over similar issues lead towards a law.
For example, observation of shadows leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
When holes in four cardboards are aligned with a torch, light passes through; when one cardboard is displaced, the light is blocked.
This experiment supports the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line, and repeated testing in different situations may establish a law.

(b) Q1.1. Calculate the number of seconds in a (a) day (b) week (c) month and state your answers using SI prefixes.
modelAnswer: (a) Displacement is the area under the speed-time graph, which is a trapezium: s = ½(u + v)t.

Therefore, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u².

written.text:
(a) State the law of conservation of energy. Explain it with the help of an example of a body falling from certain height in terms of its potential energy and kinetic energy.
(b) A force of 100 N is applied perpendicularly on a spanner at a distance of 10 cm from a nut. Find the torque produced by the force.
modelAnswer: (a) The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form into another.
At a certain height, a body has maximum potential energy and zero kinetic energy if it is at rest.
As the body falls, its potential energy decreases and is converted into kinetic energy, which increases.
Just before reaching the ground, its kinetic energy is maximum and its potential energy is minimum; the total mechanical energy remains constant if air resistance is neglected.
(b) Given: F = 100 N; r = 10 cm = 0.10 m
Formula: τ = F × r
Substitution: τ = 100 N × 0.10 m
Therefore, the torque is 10 N m.

written.text:
(a) Explain the working process of hydraulic press.
(b) A motor boat moves at a steady speed of 4 ms⁻¹. Water resistance acting on it is 4000 N. Calculate power of its engine.
modelAnswer: (a) A hydraulic press works on Pascal’s principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions.
It consists of two pistons of different cross-sectional areas connected by a pipe containing an enclosed liquid.
A force F1 on the smaller piston of area A1 produces pressure P = F1/A1 in the liquid.
The same pressure acts on the larger piston, so F2/A2 = F1/A1.
Because A2 > A1, F2 > F1; the larger force can lift or press a heavy load.
(b) Given: speed, v = 4 m s^-1; water resistance, F = 4000 N.
Since the boat moves at steady speed, the engine force balances the water resistance: F = 4000 N.
Power, P = Fv.
The power of the engine is 16000 W (16 kW).

written.text: You are provided a metre scale and a bundle of pencils; how can the diameter of a pencil be measured using the metre scale with the same precision as that of Vernier Callipers? Describe briefly.
modelAnswer: Place a known number of pencils tightly side by side in a straight row.
Measure the total width of the row with the metre scale.
Divide the total width by the number of pencils.
The quotient is the diameter of one pencil, measured more precisely by using the combined width.

written.text: Give three examples of derived unit in SI. How are they derived from base units? Describe briefly.

Derived units are formed by combining base units according to the definitions of the quantities.

written.text: Differentiate between precision and accuracy of a measurement with examples.
modelAnswer: Precision describes how close repeated measurements are to one another.
Accuracy describes how close a measurement is to the true value.
For example, repeated readings of 5.1 cm, 5.1 cm and 5.2 cm are precise; if the true value is 5.1 cm, they are also accurate.
A set of readings can be precise but inaccurate if they agree with one another but differ from the true value.

modelAnswer: (a) A screw gauge is used to measure very small lengths, such as the diameter of a wire or the thickness of a sheet.
It consists of a U-shaped frame, an anvil, a movable spindle, a main scale and a circular scale; the ratchet helps apply uniform pressure.

(b) Base quantities are independent quantities and cannot be derived from other quantities.
Derived quantities are obtained from base quantities.
The SI base units are:
Length: metre (m); mass: kilogram (kg); time: second (s); temperature: kelvin (K); electric current: ampere (A); intensity of light: candela (cd); amount of substance: mole (mol).

written.text: Derive third equation of motion with the help of speed-time graph.
modelAnswer: Let the initial speed be u, the final speed be v, the time be t, the acceleration be a, and the displacement be s.
From the speed-time graph, displacement equals the area under the graph: s = ut + 1/2(v − u)t = 1/2(u + v)t.
From the first equation of motion, v = u + at, so t = (v − u)/a.
Substitute for t: s = 1/2(u + v)(v − u)/a = (v² − u²)/(2a).
Therefore, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u².
Hence, v² = u² + 2as.

written.text: A cyclist completes half round of a circular track of radius 318 m in 1.5 minutes. Find its speed and velocity.
modelAnswer: Given: radius r = 318 m; time t = 1.5 min = 90 s.
Distance travelled in half a round = πr = 3.14 × 318 m = 998.52 m.
Speed = distance ÷ time = 998.52 m ÷ 90 s = 11.1 m/s.
Displacement = diameter = 2r = 2 × 318 m = 636 m.
Average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 636 m ÷ 90 s = 7.07 m/s, along the diameter towards the opposite point.
Speed = 11.1 m/s; average velocity = 7.07 m/s along the diameter.
Speed is the distance travelled per unit time; average velocity is the displacement per unit time in the displacement’s direction.

written.text: How can third equation of motion be derived graphically?
modelAnswer: The displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph.
The area of the trapezium is s = (u + v)t/2.
The slope of the graph gives acceleration: a = (v − u)/t.
Therefore, t = (v − u)/a.
Substituting in the displacement equation: s = (u + v)(v − u)/2a.
Thus, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u².
Therefore, v² = u² + 2as.

written.text: Derive third equation of motion with the help of graph.
modelAnswer: Draw a velocity-time graph with time on the horizontal axis, velocity on the vertical axis, and a straight line from velocity u at time 0 to velocity v at time t.
The displacement s is the area under the velocity-time graph, which is a trapezium.
Area of trapezium: s = 1/2 (u + v)t
Acceleration: a = (v − u)/t, so t = (v − u)/a
Substitute for t: s = 1/2 (u + v)(v − u)/a
Multiply by 2a: 2as = (u + v)(v − u)
Use the difference of squares: 2as = v² − u²
Therefore, v² = u² + 2as

written.text: Describe different types of motion. Also give examples.
modelAnswer: There are three general types of motion: translatory, rotatory and vibratory.
If every particle of a body moves uniformly in the same direction, it is called translatory motion; the motion of a train or a car is an example.
Translatory motion can be linear, random or circular: a freely falling body is linear, a bee moving along an irregular path is random, and a Ferris wheel is circular.
If each point of a body moves around a fixed point (axis), the motion is called rotatory motion; an electric fan or a top is an example.
When a body repeats its to and fro motion about a fixed position, the motion is called vibratory motion; a swing is an example.

written.text: What are distance- time graph and speed-time graph?
modelAnswer: A distance-time graph shows the relation between distance S and time t taken by a moving body.

written.text: What do gradients of distance-time graph and speed-time graph represent? Explain it by drawing diagrams.
modelAnswer: Gradient = change in vertical-axis quantity/change in horizontal-axis quantity.
For a distance-time graph, gradient = change in distance/change in time = speed.
For a speed-time graph, gradient = change in speed/change in time = acceleration.

written.text: The figure given below shows the distance - time graph for the travel of a cyclist. Find the velocities for the segments a, b and c. [FIGURE: Distance - time graph with vertical axis labelled “Distance → S (km)” and horizontal axis labelled “Time → t (min)”. The vertical scale is 0 to 2.0 in increments of 0.2; the horizontal scale is 0 to 20 in increments of 2. Segment a rises from (0, 0) to (6, 2.0), segment b is horizontal from (6, 2.0) to (10, 2.0), and segment c falls from (10, 2.0) to (20, 0).]
modelAnswer: Gradient = (change in distance)/(change in time)
For segment a: (2.0 − 0)/(6 − 0) = 1/3 km min⁻¹ = 20 km h⁻¹
For segment b: (2.0 − 2.0)/(10 − 6) = 0 km min⁻¹ = 0 km h⁻¹
For segment c: (0 − 2.0)/(20 − 10) = −0.2 km min⁻¹ = −12 km h⁻¹
Therefore, a = 20 km h⁻¹; b = 0 km h⁻¹; c = −12 km h⁻¹.

written.text: How equations of motion can be applied to the bodies moving under the action of gravity?
modelAnswer: Use the equations of motion: v_f = v_i + at.
S = v_i t + 1/2 at².
2aS = v_f² − v_i².
For motion under gravity, put a = g, with its sign set by the direction of acceleration.
Take the direction of initial velocity as positive; quantities in the opposite direction are negative.

written.text: How equations of motion can be applied to the bodies moving under the action of gravity?
modelAnswer: Since freely falling bodies move vertically downwards in a straight line with uniform acceleration g, the three equations of motion can be applied.
Replace acceleration a by gravitational acceleration g in the equations of motion:
v_f = v_i + gt
S = v_i t + ½gt²
2gS = v_f² − v_i²
Take g positive downward; quantities opposite to the acceleration are negative.
For a body released from a height, vᵢ = 0.
For a body thrown vertically upward, g is negative and v_f = 0 at the highest point.

written.text: Falling objects near the Earth have the same constant acceleration. Does this imply that a heavier object will fall faster than a lighter object?
modelAnswer: No. A heavier object will not fall faster than a lighter object.

modelAnswer: (i) No. With constant velocity, the change in velocity is zero, so acceleration is zero.

written.text: Distance and displacement may or may not be equal in magnitude. Explain this statement.
modelAnswer: Distance is the total length of the path travelled, while displacement is the change in position in a specified direction.
If an object moves along a straight line in one direction, distance and displacement are equal in magnitude.
If the object changes direction or follows a curved path, the distance is greater than the magnitude of the displacement.

rubric.description: Explain when they are unequal.
rubric.why: A changed path or direction makes the total path longer than the net change in position.
rubric.how: State that displacement magnitude is less than distance when the path is not a straight one-way path.

written.text: When a bullet is fired, its velocity with which it leaves the barrel is called the muzzle velocity of the gun. The muzzle velocity of one gun with a longer barrel is lesser than that of another gun with a shorter barrel. In which gun is the acceleration of the bullet larger? Explain your answer.
modelAnswer: For a bullet starting from rest, v² = u² + 2as and u = 0, so a = v²/(2s).
The question states that the longer-barrel gun has the smaller muzzle velocity; the acceleration comparison depends on both v² and barrel length.

With the usual textbook assumption that the compared muzzle velocities and barrel lengths give the shorter-barrel case the larger value of v²/(2s), the bullet's acceleration is larger in the shorter-barrel gun.

modelAnswer: Yes, it is possible.
The object may move in the negative direction during part of the trip.
If its total displacement for the complete trip is positive, its average velocity is positive even though its instantaneous velocity was negative at some time.

written.text: A ball is thrown vertically upward with velocity v. It returns to the ground in time T. Which of the following graphs correctly represents the motion? Explain your reasoning.
modelAnswer: Graph (c) is correct.
Taking upward as positive, the initial velocity is +v and the acceleration due to gravity is constant and downward.
The velocity therefore decreases linearly, becomes zero at the highest point at T/2, and is negative as the ball returns to the ground.

modelAnswer: Yes.

written.text:
(a) Derive third equation of motion with the help of speed-time graph.
(b) A train moves with a uniform velocity of 36 km h⁻¹ for 10 s. Find the distance travelled by it.
modelAnswer: (a) Let the initial speed be u, the final speed be v, the time be t, the acceleration be a, and the displacement be s.
From the speed-time graph, displacement equals the area under the graph: s = ut + 1/2(v − u)t = 1/2(u + v)t.
From the first equation of motion, v = u + at, so t = (v − u)/a.
Substitute for t: s = 1/2(u + v)(v − u)/a = (v² − u²)/(2a).
Therefore, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u².
Hence, v² = u² + 2as.
(b) Given: v = 36 km h⁻¹ = 10 m s⁻¹, t = 10 s.
Formula: s = vt.
Substitution: s = (10 m s⁻¹)(10 s).

written.text:
(a) Derive the third Equation of Motion with the help of Speed-Time graph.
(b) A cyclist completes half round of a circular track of radius 318 m in 1.5 minutes. Find its speed and velocity.
modelAnswer: (a) Displacement is the area under the speed-time graph, which is a trapezium: s = ½(u + v)t.
From the first equation of motion, v = u + at, so t = (v − u)/a.
Substitute for t: s = ½(u + v)(v − u)/a.
Therefore, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u².
Hence, v² = u² + 2as.
(b) Given: radius r = 318 m; time t = 1.5 min = 90 s.
Distance travelled in half a round = πr = 3.14 × 318 m = 998.52 m.
Speed = distance ÷ time = 998.52 m ÷ 90 s = 11.1 m/s.
Displacement = diameter = 2r = 2 × 318 m = 636 m.
Average velocity = displacement ÷ time = 636 m ÷ 90 s = 7.07 m/s, along the diameter towards the opposite point.
Speed = 11.1 m/s; average velocity = 7.07 m/s along the diameter.
Speed is the distance travelled per unit time; average velocity is the displacement per unit time in the displacement’s direction.

written.text: How much time is required to change 22 Ns momentum by a force of 20 N?

written.text: A cyclist of mass 40kg exerts a force of 200N to move his bicycle with an acceleration of 3ms⁻². How much is the force of friction between the road and the tyres?
modelAnswer: Given: m = 40 kg, applied force = 200 N, a = 3 m s⁻².
Net force, F = ma = 40 kg × 3 m s⁻² = 120 N.
Applied force − friction force = net force.
Friction force = 200 N − 120 N = 80 N.
The force of friction is 80 N, opposite to the motion.

written.text: State and explain law of conservation of momentum.
modelAnswer: For an isolated system, if no external force acts on it, its total momentum remains constant.
During an interaction between two bodies, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite: F1 = -F2.
Since force is the rate of change of momentum, the changes in the bodies’ momenta are equal and opposite.
Therefore, the total momentum before interaction equals the total momentum after interaction: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2.

written.text: State Law of Conservation of Momentum. Explain it with Balls Example.
modelAnswer: The total momentum of an isolated system remains constant, provided no external force acts on it.
Thus, total momentum before interaction = total momentum after interaction.
For two balls of masses m₁ and m₂, with initial velocities u₁ and u₂ and final velocities v₁ and v₂:
m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
When two balls collide, one ball may lose momentum while the other gains it; the total momentum of both balls remains unchanged.

rubric.description: Explains how the collision demonstrates conservation.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the momentum lost by one ball is gained by the other, so their total momentum remains unchanged.

written.text: State and prove law of Conservation of momentum.
modelAnswer: Consider two bodies of masses m₁ and m₂ with initial velocities u₁ and u₂ and final velocities v₁ and v₂.
During their interaction, the forces on them are F₁₂ and F₂₁, acting for the same time interval Δt.
By Newton’s third law, the interaction forces are equal and opposite: F₁₂ = −F₂₁.
Using force as the rate of change of momentum: (m₁v₁ − m₁u₁)/Δt = −(m₂v₂ − m₂u₂)/Δt.
Rearranging gives m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Therefore, total initial momentum equals total final momentum. The total momentum remains constant when no external force acts.

written.text: State Law of conservation of momentum and also derive its equation.
modelAnswer: The law of conservation of momentum states that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant, provided no external force acts on it.
Consider two bodies of masses m1 and m2 moving with initial velocities u1 and u2; after interaction, their velocities are v1 and v2.

Rearranging gives m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2; hence total initial momentum equals total final momentum.

written.text: Find out the relation for acceleration and tension of two bodies attached to the ends of string when one moves vertically and other moves horizontally.

written.text: How can you relate a force with the change of momentum of a body and prove that: (P_f − P_i)/t = F

Since P_i = mu and P_f = mv, F = (mv − mu)/t = (P_f − P_i)/t.

written.text: State and explain the Law of Conservation of momentum with the help of spheres experiment.
modelAnswer: Law: When no net external force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant.
Take two spheres on a smooth horizontal surface: sphere 1 moves with velocity u1 and sphere 2 is initially at rest (u2 = 0).
They collide and then move with velocities v1 and v2.
Before collision, total momentum = m1u1 + m2u2; after collision, total momentum = m1v1 + m2v2.
Therefore, m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2: the momentum lost by one sphere is gained by the other, and total momentum is conserved.

written.text: A force acting on a body of mass 5kg produces acceleration of 10ms⁻². What acceleration the same force will produce in a body of mass 8kg?
modelAnswer: Given: m₁ = 5 kg, a₁ = 10 m/s², m₂ = 8 kg.
Force on the first body: F = m₁a₁.
F = 5 kg × 10 m/s² = 50 N.
For the second body: a₂ = F/m₂.
a₂ = 50 N / 8 kg = 6.25 m/s².
The acceleration produced is 6.25 m/s².

written.text: State and explain the principle of conservation of momentum.
modelAnswer: The principle of conservation of momentum states that:
If no external force acts on an isolated system, the final total momentum of the system is equal to the initial total momentum of the system.
Total momentum of the system before collision = Total momentum of the system after collision
m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = m₁v′₁ + m₂v′₂
Momentum may transfer from one object to another, but the total momentum of the system remains the same.

written.text:
(a) State and explain law of conservation of momentum.
(b) Find the acceleration produced by a force of 100N in a mass of 50kg.
modelAnswer: (a) For an isolated system, if no external force acts on it, its total momentum remains constant.
During an interaction between two bodies, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite: F1 = -F2.
Since force is the rate of change of momentum, the changes in the bodies’ momenta are equal and opposite.
Therefore, the total momentum before interaction equals the total momentum after interaction: m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2.
(b) Given: F = 100 N, m = 50 kg
Formula: a = F/m
Substitution: a = 100 N / 50 kg
Answer: a = 2 m/s²

written.text:

modelAnswer: (a) Mass is the amount of matter in a body; weight is the gravitational force acting on it.
Mass is a scalar quantity; weight is a vector quantity.
The SI unit of mass is kilogram (kg); the SI unit of weight is newton (N).
Mass remains constant with location; weight changes when gravitational field strength changes.
(b) Given: m = 40 kg, applied force = 200 N, a = 3 m s⁻².
Net force, F = ma = 40 kg × 3 m s⁻² = 120 N.
Applied force − friction force = net force.
Friction force = 200 N − 120 N = 80 N.
The force of friction is 80 N, opposite to the motion.

In neutral equilibrium, a small displacement leaves the body in equilibrium at its new position.

written.text: Define Equilibrium. Explain states of equilibrium.
modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force and the resultant torque acting on it are both zero.

Unstable equilibrium: after a small displacement, the body moves farther from its original position; for example, a ball balanced on top of a hill.
Neutral equilibrium: after a small displacement, the body remains in its new position; for example, a ball on a horizontal surface.

written.text: Find a force from its perpendicular components by using a figure.

written.text: Discuss the concepts of stability and centre of gravity in relation to objects toppling over. Provide an example where an object’s centre of gravity affects its stability, and explain how altering its base of support can influence stability.
modelAnswer: An object topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base of support.
An object with a higher centre of gravity is easier to topple.

Widening the base of support makes an object more stable because the vertical line through its centre of gravity can move farther before falling outside the base.

written.text: Why an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium?

Therefore, an accelerated body cannot be considered in equilibrium.

written.text: How can you prove that the centripetal force always acts perpendicular to velocity?
modelAnswer: The velocity at any point on a circular path is directed along the tangent.
If the force were not perpendicular to velocity, it would have a component in the direction of velocity.
This component would change the magnitude of velocity.
As the body moves with constant speed, this component is zero: F cos 90° = 0.
Therefore, the centripetal force acts perpendicular to velocity.

written.text:
(a) Determine a force from its perpendicular components.
(b) Find the Perpendicular Components of a Force of 50 N making an angle of 30° with x-axis.
modelAnswer: (a) Let the perpendicular force components be Fx and Fy.
The resultant force R is the diagonal of the right-angled triangle formed by the components.
By Pythagoras' theorem, R^2 = Fx^2 + Fy^2.
Therefore, the magnitude is R = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2).
If θ is measured from Fx, its direction is given by tan θ = Fy/Fx, so θ = tan^-1(Fy/Fx).
(b) Given: F = 50 N, θ = 30° to the x-axis.
Horizontal component: Fx = F cos θ = (50 N) cos 30° = 43.3 N.
Vertical component: Fy = F sin θ = (50 N) sin 30° = 25 N.
The perpendicular components are 43.3 N along the x-axis and 25 N along the y-axis.

written.text:
(a) Define Resolution of forces. How can a force F be resolved into its perpendicular components?
(b) A force is acting on a body making an angle of 30° with the horizontal. The horizontal component of the force is 20 N. Find the force
modelAnswer: (a) Resolution of forces is the process of splitting a force into components along specified directions, whose combined effect is the same as that of the original force.
For a force F making an angle θ with the horizontal, the perpendicular components are horizontal and vertical.
Horizontal component: Fx = F cos θ
Vertical component: Fy = F sin θ
(b) Given: horizontal component F_x = 20 N, angle theta = 30 degrees
Formula: F_x = F*cos(theta)
Rearranging: F = F_x/cos(theta)
Substitution: F = 20/cos(30) N = 23.1 N
Answer: The force is approximately 23.1 N.

written.text: What is meant by kinetic energy? Derive its equation.
modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
The work done to bring a body from rest to speed v is its kinetic energy.
W = Fs and F = ma, so W = mas.
For a body starting from rest, v² = u² + 2as and u = 0; therefore, s = v²/(2a).
W = ma × v²/(2a) = 1/2mv².
Therefore, kinetic energy, KE = 1/2mv².

written.text: Define kinetic energy. Derive its mathematical equation.

Work done on the object is W = Fs, and F = ma; therefore W = mas.
