written.text:
(a) What is meant by kinetic energy? Derive its equation.
(b) Calculate the power of a pump which can lift 200 kg of water through a height of 6 m in 10 seconds.
modelAnswer: (a) Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
The work done to bring a body from rest to speed v is its kinetic energy.
W = Fs and F = ma, so W = mas.
For a body starting from rest, v² = u² + 2as and u = 0; therefore, s = v²/(2a).
W = ma × v²/(2a) = 1/2mv².
Therefore, kinetic energy, KE = 1/2mv².
(b) Given: m = 200 kg, h = 6 m, t = 10 s and g = 10 m s⁻².
Work done in lifting the water: W = mgh.
Power: P = W/t = mgh/t.
Substituting: P = (200 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 6 m)/(10 s) = 1200 W.
The power of the pump is 1200 W.

(a) State the law of conservation of energy. Explain it with the help of an example of a body falling from certain height in terms of its potential energy and kinetic energy.
(b) A motor boat moves at a steady speed of 4ms⁻¹. Water resistance acting on it is 4000N. Calculate the power of its engine.
modelAnswer: (a) The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form into another.
At a certain height, a body has maximum potential energy and zero kinetic energy if it is at rest.
As the body falls, its potential energy decreases and is converted into kinetic energy, which increases.
Just before reaching the ground, its kinetic energy is maximum and its potential energy is minimum; the total mechanical energy remains constant if air resistance is neglected.
(b) Given: v = 4 m s⁻¹, water resistance = 4000 N.
Since the boat moves at steady speed, the engine force balances the water resistance: F = 4000 N.
Power, P = Fv.
The power of the engine is 16000 W (16 kW).

written.text: Explain the working process of hydraulic press.
modelAnswer: A hydraulic press works on Pascal’s principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions.
It consists of two pistons of different cross-sectional areas connected by a pipe containing an enclosed liquid.
A force F1 on the smaller piston of area A1 produces pressure P = F1/A1 in the liquid.
The same pressure acts on the larger piston, so F2/A2 = F1/A1.
Because A2 > A1, F2 > F1; the larger force can lift or press a heavy load.

written.text: Explain the pressure in liquids and derive its formula (P = ρgh).
modelAnswer: Consider a liquid column of height h and cross-sectional area A.
Volume of the column = Ah.
If the liquid density is ρ, mass of the column = ρ × Ah = ρAh.
Weight of the column, F = mg = ρAhg.
Pressure, P = force ÷ area = F/A.
P = ρAhg/A.
Therefore, P = ρgh.

written.text: State Pascal's law and derive an equation by using hydraulic press.
modelAnswer: Pascal’s law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished in every direction throughout the fluid and to the walls of its container.
In a hydraulic press, let F1 and A1 be the force and area of the small piston, and F2 and A2 those of the large piston.
By Pascal’s law, the pressures at the pistons are equal: P1 = P2.
Since pressure P = F/A, F1/A1 = F2/A2.
Therefore, F2 = F1A2/A1.

written.text: State Pascal’s Law and Explain the working of Hydraulic Press.
modelAnswer: Pascal’s Law: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished in all directions.
A hydraulic press has a small piston of area A1 and a large piston of area A2 connected by an enclosed liquid.
A force F1 on the small piston produces pressure P = F1/A1 in the liquid.

written.text:
A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below: For each arrangement, complete the table by determining:
(i) the total extension in terms of x.
(ii) the spring constant in terms of k. | Arrangement | Total Extension x | Spring constant (k) of the arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom.] | | |
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.] | | |
modelAnswer: For one spring, L = kx.
Series: each spring carries load L, so each extends by x.
Total extension in series = x + x = 2x.
Spring constant in series = L/(2x) = kx/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the identical springs share the load equally, so each carries L/2.
Extension of each spring = (L/2)/k = x/2; hence total extension = x/2.
Spring constant in parallel = L/(x/2) = 2L/x = 2k.

rubric.why: The equivalent spring constant must produce extension 2x under load L.
rubric.how: Use k arrangement = L/(2x) and L = kx, giving k/2.

written.text: Example 6.4: The diameters of the pistons of a hydraulic press are 5 cm and 25 cm respectively. A normal force of 160 N is applied on the smaller piston, what will be the pressure exerted by this force on the bigger piston? How much weight can be lifted by the other piston?

A₁ = πr₁² and A₂ = πr₂²

According to Pascal's law, F₁/A₁ = w/A₂
w = F₁A₂/A₁ = F₁πr₂²/(πr₁²) = F₁ × r₂²/r₁²
Pressure transmitted = 8.15 × 10⁴ Pa; weight lifted = 4000 N = 4 kN.

written.text:
A spring having spring constant k hangs vertically from a fixed point. A load of weight L, when hung from the spring, causes an extension x, the elastic limit of the spring is not exceeded. Some identical springs, each with spring constant k, are arranged as shown below: For each arrangement, complete the table by determining:
(i) the total extension in terms of x.
(ii) the spring constant in terms of k. | Arrangement | Total Extension x | Spring constant (k) of the arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged vertically in series, hanging from a fixed support, with a load labelled L at the bottom.] | | |
| [FIGURE: Two springs arranged in parallel between a fixed support and a horizontal bar, with a load labelled L hanging from the bar.] | | |
modelAnswer: One spring under load L extends by x, so L = kx.
Series: the same load acts on each spring, so each extends by x.
Series total extension = x + x = 2x; equivalent k = L/(2x) = k/2.
Parallel: the load is shared equally, so each spring supports L/2.
Extension of each spring = (L/2)/k = x/2; both have the same total extension x/2.
Parallel equivalent spring constant = L/(x/2) = 2k.

written.text:
(a) Prove that: Upthrust of liquid = ρ g V
(b) The Density of Air is 1.3 Kgm⁻³. Find the Mass of Air in a room measuring 8 m × 5 m × 4 m.
modelAnswer: (a) Consider a body of height h and cross-sectional area A immersed in a liquid of density ρ.
Let P₁ and P₂ be the pressures on its upper and lower surfaces, respectively.
Pressure difference, P₂ − P₁ = ρgh
Upthrust, F = (P₂ − P₁)A = ρghA
Volume of displaced liquid, V = Ah
Therefore, upthrust of liquid, F = ρgV
(b) Given: ρ = 1.3 kg m⁻³; room dimensions = 8 m × 5 m × 4 m.
Volume of room: V = 8 m × 5 m × 4 m = 160 m³.
Formula: m = ρV.
Substitution: m = 1.3 kg m⁻³ × 160 m³ = 208 kg.
Mass of air in the room = 208 kg.

written.text:
(a) Explain the working process of hydraulic press.
(b) A wooden block measuring 40cm × 10cm × 5cm has a mass 850g. Find the density of wood.
modelAnswer: (a) A hydraulic press works on Pascal’s principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions.
It consists of two pistons of different cross-sectional areas connected by a pipe containing an enclosed liquid.
A force F1 on the smaller piston of area A1 produces pressure P = F1/A1 in the liquid.
The same pressure acts on the larger piston, so F2/A2 = F1/A1.
Because A2 > A1, F2 > F1; the larger force can lift or press a heavy load.
(b) Given: m = 850 g = 0.850 kg.
Dimensions: 40 cm = 0.40 m, 10 cm = 0.10 m, 5 cm = 0.05 m.
Formula: density, ρ = m / V.
Substitution: ρ = 0.850 kg / 0.002 m³ = 425 kg m⁻³.
Answer: the density of the wood is 425 kg m⁻³.

written.text: An electric heater supplies heat at the rate of 1000 Joules per second. How much time is required to raise the temperature of 200 g of water from 20 °C to 90 °C?

Power: P = Q/t, so t = Q/P.

written.text: Why is mercury usually preferred to alcohol as a thermometric liquid?

For greater accuracy, alcohol can be used as its expansivity is six times more than mercury.
But alcohol has range limitation to higher temperature measurements due to its low boiling point (78°C).

written.text: Describe the main points of particle theory of matter which differentiate solids, liquids and gases.
modelAnswer: Matter consists of tiny particles.
In a solid, particles are very closely packed, strongly attracted and vibrate about fixed mean positions; a solid has fixed shape and volume.
In a liquid, particles are close together but can move past one another; a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
In a gas, particles are far apart, weakly attracted and move freely in random directions; a gas has neither fixed shape nor fixed volume.
Thus, particle spacing, motion and intermolecular forces differentiate solids, liquids and gases.

written.text:
(a) Explain Celsius scale and Fahrenheit scale with the figures.
(b) Temperature of water in a beaker is 80°C. What is its value in Fahrenheit scale?
modelAnswer: (a) The Celsius scale has two fixed points: the ice point is 0°C and the steam point is 100°C.
The interval between these points is divided into 100 equal divisions.
Figure (Celsius): 100°C — steam point; 100 equal divisions; 0°C — ice point.
The Fahrenheit scale has two fixed points: the ice point is 32°F and the steam point is 212°F.
The interval between these points is divided into 180 equal divisions.
Figure (Fahrenheit): 212°F — steam point; 180 equal divisions; 32°F — ice point.
(b) Given: C = 80°C.
Formula: F = (9/5)C + 32.
Substitution: F = (9/5)(80) + 32.
Calculation: F = 144 + 32.
Therefore, F = 176°F.

written.text: Differentiate between paramagnetic, diamagnetic and ferromagnetic materials with reference to the domain theory.
modelAnswer: In paramagnetic materials, the orbital and spin fields support one another, so each atom has a resultant magnetic field and behaves like a tiny magnet.
Examples are aluminium and lithium.
In diamagnetic materials, the orbital and spin fields add up to zero, so each atom has no resultant field.
Examples are copper, bismuth and water.
In ferromagnetic materials, electron spins in large groups of neighbouring atoms are naturally aligned parallel to each other.
These groups form highly magnetized domains, each of which behaves as a small magnet with its own north and south poles.

Steel retains this alignment and is used to make permanent magnets.

written.text: What are the main branches of Physics? State briefly.
modelAnswer: Mechanics: It is a study of motion and the physical effects which influence motion.
Heat and thermodynamics: It deal with the thermal energy possessed by the materials and it is used when it flows from one body to another.
Acoustics: It deals with the nature and physical aspects of audible sound energy.
Optics: It deal with the physical aspects of visible light.
Electromagnetism: It is the study of electromagnetic phenomenon and mutual relationship between electric current and magnetic field.
Quantum Mechanics: It explains the behaviour of particles at the atomic and subatomic level.

Relativistic Mechanics: It explains how space and time are not absolute quantities but related to observer. It describes the relationship between them and how they are influenced by gravity and speed.
Nuclear Physics: It is the study of the properties of nuclei of the atoms.
Particle Physics: It is the study of subatomic particles and elementary particles which are basic building blocks of matter.
Astronomy: It is study of distribution of celestial bodies like planets, stars and galaxies.
Cosmology: It explores the large structure and evolution of the universe.
Solid State Physics: It is the study of some specific properties of matter in solid form.

written.text: What is scientific method? Describe its main steps with examples.
modelAnswer: Scientific method is a systematic approach used to search for truth of an issue and problem solving regarding natural and physical world.
First, identify a problem and gather information by observation.
Next, propose a hypothesis and perform an experiment or collect evidence to test it.
Record, organize and analyse the data to reach a conclusion called a theory; repeated tests of the theory over similar issues lead towards a law.
For example, observation of shadows leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
When holes in four cardboards are aligned with a torch, light passes through; when one cardboard is displaced, the light is blocked.
This experiment supports the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line, and repeated testing in different situations may establish a law.

Nuclear Physics: It is the study of the properties of nuclei of the atoms.
Particle Physics: It is the study of subatomic particles and elementary particles which are basic building blocks of matter.
Astronomy: It is study of distribution of celestial bodies like planets, stars and galaxies.
Cosmology: It explores the large structure and evolution of the universe.
Solid State Physics: It is the study of some specific properties of matter in solid form.

written.text:
(a) Is the theory of science an ultimate truth? Describe briefly.
(b) What is scientific method? Describe its main steps with examples.
modelAnswer: (a) No, a scientific theory is not an ultimate truth.
Theories are man-made ideas about the way things work, based on available evidence.
They may be disproved or modified when future advances in science bring fresh facts and new insights about the natural and physical world.
(b) Scientific method is a systematic approach used to search for truth of an issue and problem solving regarding natural and physical world.
First, identify a problem and gather information by observation.
Next, propose a hypothesis and perform an experiment or collect evidence to test it.
Record, organize and analyse the data to reach a conclusion called a theory; repeated tests of the theory over similar issues lead towards a law.
For example, observation of shadows leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
When holes in four cardboards are aligned with a torch, light passes through; when one cardboard is displaced, the light is blocked.
This experiment supports the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line, and repeated testing in different situations may establish a law.

written.text:
(a) Determine a force from its perpendicular components.
(b) The Density of Air is 1.3 Kgm⁻³. Find the Mass of Air in a room measuring 8 m × 5 m × 4 m.
modelAnswer: (a) Let the perpendicular force components be Fx and Fy.
The resultant force R is the diagonal of the right-angled triangle formed by the components.
By Pythagoras' theorem, R^2 = Fx^2 + Fy^2.
Therefore, the magnitude is R = sqrt(Fx^2 + Fy^2).
If θ is measured from Fx, its direction is given by tan θ = Fy/Fx, so θ = tan^-1(Fy/Fx).
(b) Given: ρ = 1.3 kg m⁻³; room dimensions = 8 m × 5 m × 4 m.
Volume of room: V = 8 m × 5 m × 4 m = 160 m³.
Formula: m = ρV.
Substitution: m = 1.3 kg m⁻³ × 160 m³ = 208 kg.
Mass of air in the room = 208 kg.

written.text:
(a) Derive the third Equation of Motion with the help of Speed-Time graph.
(b) Q1.1. Calculate the number of seconds in a (a) day (b) week (c) month and state your answers using SI prefixes.
modelAnswer: (a) Displacement is the area under the speed-time graph, which is a trapezium: s = ½(u + v)t.
From the first equation of motion, v = u + at, so t = (v − u)/a.
Substitute for t: s = ½(u + v)(v − u)/a.
Therefore, 2as = (u + v)(v − u) = v² − u².
Hence, v² = u² + 2as.

written.text:
(a) State the law of conservation of energy. Explain it with the help of an example of a body falling from certain height in terms of its potential energy and kinetic energy.
(b) A force of 100 N is applied perpendicularly on a spanner at a distance of 10 cm from a nut. Find the torque produced by the force.
modelAnswer: (a) The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be transformed from one form into another.
At a certain height, a body has maximum potential energy and zero kinetic energy if it is at rest.
As the body falls, its potential energy decreases and is converted into kinetic energy, which increases.
Just before reaching the ground, its kinetic energy is maximum and its potential energy is minimum; the total mechanical energy remains constant if air resistance is neglected.
(b) Given: F = 100 N; r = 10 cm = 0.10 m
Formula: τ = F × r
Substitution: τ = 100 N × 0.10 m
Therefore, the torque is 10 N m.

written.text:
(a) How can you identify whether an object is a magnet or a magnetic material?
(b) Temperature of water in a beaker is 80°C. What is its value in Fahrenheit scale?
modelAnswer: (a) Bring one end of the object close to any pole of a suspended bar magnet.
If it is attracted, it may be the opposite pole of a magnet or a magnetic material.
Bring the same end of the object close to the other pole of the suspended magnet.
If it is attracted again, the object is a magnetic material, not a magnet.
If it is repelled by the other end, the object is a magnet.
Repulsion between like poles is the real test for identifying a magnet.
(b) Given: C = 80°C.
Formula: F = (9/5)C + 32.
Substitution: F = (9/5)(80) + 32.
Calculation: F = 144 + 32.
Therefore, F = 176°F.

written.text:
(a) Describe any four differences between mass and weight.
(b) A train starts from rest. It moves through 1 km in 100 second with uniform acceleration. What will be its speed at the end of 100 second.
modelAnswer: (a) Mass is the amount of matter in a body; weight is the gravitational force acting on it.
Mass is a scalar quantity; weight is a vector quantity.
The SI unit of mass is kilogram (kg); the SI unit of weight is newton (N).
Mass remains constant with location; weight changes when gravitational field strength changes.
(b) Given: Initial velocity, u = 0 m/s; distance, s = 1 km = 1000 m; time, t = 100 s.
Required: Final velocity, v.
Formula: s = (u + v)t/2, so v = 2s/t − u.
Substitution: v = 2(1000 m)/(100 s) − 0 m/s = 20 m/s.
Answer: The train’s speed at the end of 100 s is 20 m/s.

written.text:
(a) Explain the working process of hydraulic press.
(b) A motor boat moves at a steady speed of 4 ms⁻¹. Water resistance acting on it is 4000 N. Calculate power of its engine.
modelAnswer: (a) A hydraulic press works on Pascal’s principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions.
It consists of two pistons of different cross-sectional areas connected by a pipe containing an enclosed liquid.
A force F1 on the smaller piston of area A1 produces pressure P = F1/A1 in the liquid.
The same pressure acts on the larger piston, so F2/A2 = F1/A1.
Because A2 > A1, F2 > F1; the larger force can lift or press a heavy load.
(b) Given: speed, v = 4 m s^-1; water resistance, F = 4000 N.
Since the boat moves at steady speed, the engine force balances the water resistance: F = 4000 N.
Power, P = Fv.
The power of the engine is 16000 W (16 kW).

modelAnswer: (a) Yes, existing laws of nature may need to change in the future.

Future advances in science may bring fresh facts and new insights.
These may lead to a theory or law being modified or disproved.
